people/albert-s-lai.content:
Dr. Albert S. Lai (賴信雄)
Dr. Albert S. Lai (賴信雄, Lai Sin-hiong) is a Taiwanese American pastor, theologian, and institution-builder who helped establish the first Taiwanese Presbyterian Church in North America and authored the landmark 1971 dissertation Toward A Community of Hope — A Mission to Formosan Community in Los Angeles, reprinted in 2025 with a 50th anniversary foreword.
Identity Snapshot

Full name: Albert S. Lai (賴信雄, Lai Sin-hiong)
Era: 1960s–2020s (active 1960s–1970s; 2025 republication at age 84+)
Geography: Taiwan → San Francisco → Los Angeles, California
Education: San Francisco Theological Seminary (doctoral dissertation); Taiwan Theological College and Seminary (TTCS)
Core roles: Pastor, theologian, seminary educator, FPCLA founding member, dissertation author

Historical Context
Dr. Lai’s life and work sit at the intersection of migration-era pastoral care and institution formation. In 1970, he participated in the founding of the Formosan Presbyterian Church in Los Angeles (FPCLA), the first Taiwanese church in North America. In 1971, he produced a doctoral dissertation that connected historical memory, migration pressure, identity tension, and communal mission. His work remains a foundational reference for Taiwanese American church history.
FPCLA Founding (1970)
Dr. Lai was among the enthusiastic believers who co-founded FPCLA under the theology and system of the United Presbyterian Church (UPCUSA, now PC(USA)). The founding involved:

Co-founders: Dr. & Mrs. Daniel Kao (高光民), Dr. & Mrs. C. C. Chen (陳昭俊), Mr. & Mrs. Norman Hsu (許彬), Dr. & Mrs. Isiah Lee (李宗派), Dr. & Mrs. Joseph T. C. Lu (盧俊哲), Mr. & Mrs. Morris Chen (陳茂雄), Mr. & Mrs. George Chen (陳進琛), Dr. & Mrs. Sze-Ya Yeh (葉思雅), Mr. & Mrs. Wang Chun Hsiung (王春雄), Dr. & Mrs. Jang Yan Wu (吳政彥), Dr. Wen-Cho Yang (楊哲), Dr. & Mrs. Justin Chen (陳有義), Meiling Lai (賴美玲), Michael Chen (陳明章), and others
Supporting pastors and elders: From the UPCUSA system including San Francisco Theological Seminary, the General Assembly of the United Presbyterian Church, the Southern California/Hawaii Presbytery, and the Pacific Presbytery
Organizing Pastor:  Chaolong Kao (高昭龍) — former TTCS faculty / Harvard Visiting Scholar; called by Presbytery of Los Angeles Southwest (Sep 1971). Distinct from co-founder Daniel Kao.
Predecessor experiment: “Taiyou Church” (太陽教會) and the Aug 1970 experimental worship led by Rev. Jonah Chang (張瑞雄)

Dissertation: Toward A Community of Hope (1971)

Primary work page: Toward A Community of Hope (work & sources)
Full text (GitHub archive): complete extract · fact sheet

Dr. Lai’s doctoral dissertation at San Francisco Theological Seminary was titled Toward A Community of Hope — A Mission to Formosan Community in Los Angeles. It was:

Theological and prophetic: Called the church to transcend being merely a haven for immigrants and become a missional community, a beacon of hope and witness to the gospel in the larger society
Six chapters: Formosan in Formosa Yesterday; Formosan in Formosa Today; Formosan in The United States; Formosan Christian Church in Los Angeles; Integration, Independence and Identity of Formosan Community; Toward a Community
Vision: The church as a “hopeful community” — not a safe retreat for insiders, but a dynamic body for the hope of the world, choosing love in adversity, service in marginality, and witness in brokenness
Significance: The first Taiwanese church in North America; FPCLA did not exist merely to bridge linguistic or cultural gaps but sought to become a “mission base” in the local community

See also the FPCLA page for Chapter IV founding timeline, budget, membership, and activities.
50th Anniversary Republication (2025)
In 2025, the dissertation was reprinted with a 50th anniversary foreword by Dr. Yunching Yeh Davis (NTPC Moderator), along with forewords from the PCT (Rev. En Sheng Pan), NTPC Historical Committee (Rev. Ching Fang Chen), Rev. Mingyuan Hsu (Good Shepherd TPC), and Rev. Pinghsi Liu (Tainan East Gate Barclay Memorial Church). The republication was published by Taiwan Church Press and the Incorporated Association of Tainan East Gate Barclay History Education Promotion.
Self-Preface (May 2025)
In his Self-Preface, Dr. Lai reflected:

“When my esteemed Rev. Mingyuan Hsu of the Los Angeles Good Shepherd Presbyterian Church in Taiwan informed me that Rev. Pinghsi Liu and his team from the Tainan East Gate Barclay Memorial Church were interested in my dissertation and wanted to translate it into Chinese for publication, I was filled with gratitude.”

He noted that existing writings about Taiwanese churches in North America all start from the 1980s, while his dissertation reflects the lives of Taiwanese and Taiwanese Christians in Southern California from the 1960s to the early 1970s — a period when Taiwan was under the Kuomintang’s White Terror, and thousands of Taiwanese students came to the US each year.
Recall the Story Behind the Dissertation
In his extended postscript written over 50 years later, Dr. Lai narrated the remarkable story of how his 1971 dissertation was rediscovered, translated, and published — a journey he could never have imagined while writing it.
Rediscovery and Publication
When the dissertation was presented to readers in 2025, Dr. Lai noted that the intended audience at the time was only about 10 people: his two thesis advisors, one project field consultant, and the seminary faculty thesis review committee. In the information-scarce 1960s, these professors had very limited understanding of Taiwan and had never heard of the Taiwanese people’s desire to “rise up” or the persecution faced by the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan.
The dissertation, presented in Chinese to Taiwanese on the island and in America more than 50 years later, was something Dr. Lai could never have imagined. It was Rev. Mingyuan Hsu of the Los Angeles Good Shepherd Presbyterian Church in Taiwan who first approached Dr. Lai, informing him that Rev. Pinghsi Liu and his team from the Tainan East Gate Barclay Memorial Church were interested in the dissertation and wanted to translate it into Chinese for publication. Dr. Lai was filled with gratitude.
The publication journey spanned from 2023 to 2025, culminating in the 50th anniversary republication by Taiwan Church Press and the Incorporated Association of Tainan East Gate Barclay History Education Promotion, with forewords from Dr. Yunching Yeh Davis (NTPC Moderator), the PCT, NTPC Historical Committee, Rev. Mingyuan Hsu, and Rev. Pinghsi Liu.
Historical Context of the Writing
Dr. Lai emphasized that the dissertation was written during one of the most tumultuous periods in modern history. As a student at San Francisco Theological Seminary from 1968 to 1972, he was immersed in the American cultural revolution — the women’s rights movement, civil rights movement, anti-Vietnam War movement, counterculture movement, the assassinations of Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert Kennedy, and the moon landing. Theology students at the time were exposed to “Feminist Theology,” “Black Theology,” “Theology of the Death of God,” “Theology of Liberation,” and “Theology of Hope.”
Simultaneously, dramatic events unfolded related to Taiwan: the expulsion of the Republic of China from the United Nations, and the April 24, 1970, incident when Peter Huang (黃文雄), a Cornell doctoral candidate, shot at Chingkuo Chiang (蔣經國) at the New York Plaza Hotel. In 1971, the ROC was expelled from the UN, and Taiwan became a “global orphan.” Nixon’s official visit to China in February 1972 further worsened Taiwan’s political situation. Dr. Lai graduated from SFTS in May 1972, during this period of profound disorientation.
Chapter VI: Toward a Community of Hope
Chapter VI of Dr. Lai’s dissertation developed the theological framework that gave the project its name. The chapter explored hope not as passive waiting but as active, shared venture — and the church as the community where hope is generated and sustained.
Hope Is Possibility
Dr. Lai defined hope as the recognition that what one hopes for is not yet possessed but is possible. He drew on Gabriel Marcel’s distinction between “hope” (the noun) and “hoping” (the verb), arguing that hoping is a psychic activity that occurs only when a person feels “caught” by the human condition — in captivity. Only when everything does not go perfectly well can hoping enter the picture.
He noted the increase in despair and “un-hope” among Formosan people in the United States, especially after Nixon’s shift on China policy. The word “hopeless” was often used by Formosans to stand for “helplessness” on one hand and “fearfulness” on the other — an inability to visualize a future in which personal identity and national independence were possible.
Hope Is Adventure
Citing Gabriel Marcel’s Homo Viator, Dr. Lai argued that hoping is a process — a psychic activity of the person, not just an idea. He quoted Roy W. Fairchild: “Hope allows one to live in uncertainty. Hope cannot predict that such and such will happen, nor claim that such and such must happen. But because the hoping person sees reality as open-ended and not fixed, he assumes that reality has resources which are as yet undiscovered and untapped. This is his risk and his adventure.”
Hope Is Sharing
A central thesis of Chapter VI was that hope is fundamentally a sharing experience. Dr. Lai wrote: “Often hope is considered an interior strength, some believe one possesses alone. But can one hope as a lone individual? … Hope is basically a sharing experience. It requires a responsive other if one is to discover real hope.”
He cited Marcel’s insight that true hoping requires an interpersonal context, and isolation leads to hopelessness and disintegration. “For human beings, mutual help is part of the nature of hope; hope is the anticipation of helpful relationship. Hope grows in a network of human caring. Theologically speaking, hope is the Holy Spirit in the Christian Church. Without the experience of the Spirit, there is no distinctly Christian understanding of hope.”
The Church as Community of Hope
Dr. Lai’s ecclesiology placed the church squarely as a “community of hope” — not a Community of the Past, not merely a Community of the Now, and not even a Community of the Future. “For hope is historical,” he wrote. “Michael Novak is right when he says, ‘To be a Christian is to be a member of historical people.’ So accordingly, hope is not to be mistaken for a futurism that flees from the burden and the joys of the present. It is not an escapist trick; it is not creating a new ‘God of the gaps’ so that we merely slip into the future the problems we cannot solve in the present. If anything, it calls us to the front line of world history as the missionary people of God.”
He drew on Dietrich Bonhoeffer’s vision of Christian life as participation in the suffering of God in the life of the world, and on Robert Lee’s conclusion that “the Christian is armed with hope and confidence, born of realism and the realization that we are temporary and fallen residents of this earth.”
Dr. Lai also drew a powerful parallel between the Formosan experience and the Israelite Exodus: “Like the Israelites of old, they search for the meaning of life. Probably this is why among Formosans, according to percentage, there are more Christians committed to the Formosan Independence Movement than non-Christians — since the phenomenon of the Formosan Independence Movement logically is a Hope Movement.”
The “Out” of Hope
Dr. Lai explored the radical implication of ekklesia — the “called-out” nature of the Christian community. To follow Christ is to venture “out of tradition, out of ‘consensus of opinion,’ out of any comfortable settling down in the shelter of the anonymous mass.” He warned against the common error of mistaking the symbol for reality — “one only looks at the finger which points out the way and then prefers to suck it comfortably, instead of following the direction it indicates.”
Conclusion: Lessons from History
Dr. Lai’s conclusion synthesized the dissertation’s critical findings across multiple dimensions:
Formosan Nationalism and Hope
Dr. Lai observed that historically, Formosans had been struggling for self-determination and national independence for almost thirty years without success. “The future of Formosan independence lies mainly in the hand of the majority itself. The real test of nationalism is a people’s willingness to fight for it. In other words, when a person is independent, a nation is independent. Realistic and dynamic hope is the key to the problems of independence, personal and national as well.”
Ethnic Church Mission
He argued that new immigrants from Formosa should not be treated as regular immigrants but as people with particular problems requiring specific pastoral care. “The goal of a church is to carry out Christian mission, not to self-support. This is especially true to a new ethnic church. Ministry concerns primarily people (person) not head-counting or real estates. The church is where a group of people can touch one another’s heart and feel they are one in the Holy Spirit.”
Experience Over Theory
Dr. Lai emphasized attending to actual experience over abstract theory: “In principle, it seems good to attend more closely to our actual experience than to theories, formulas or doctrine which purports to articulate and to direct that experience. For experience is in principle richer, more complex, and more full of compass.”
The Biblical Hope Movement
A striking conclusion was his observation that “according to percentage there are much more Christians than non-Christians involved in the Formosan Hope Movement — Formosan Independence Movement.” He concluded that this phenomenon stemmed from a Biblical Hope Movement, with Formosan activists identifying contemporary history with the Israelite Exodus and identifying themselves with Abraham, Moses, Joshua, and Jesus.
Hope vs. Hopelessness
Dr. Lai articulated a crucial distinction: “It is when we mix hope with what is hopeless that we become filled with hopelessness. It is the recognition that some ways are hopeless that open up for us the way to find hope. The important thing is not to think that all things can be hoped for but to keep the hopeless out of hope, to separate the impossible from the possible.”
He quoted Paul Freire: “This climate of hope is born at the exact moment when a given society begins to turn upon itself and finds out that it is not finished, that there is an infinite number of tasks to be accomplished. The hopelessness and pessimism which existed before about its present and future, as well as the naïve optimism, give place to a critical optimism, to hope.”
The Missing 50 Years: Dr. Lai’s Personal Journey
The “Missing 50 Years” section traces Dr. Lai’s extraordinary life after completing his doctorate in May 1972 — a period during which he largely disappeared from public Taiwanese church circles.
Graduation and Disappearance
Dr. Lai completed his doctoral degree in May 1972. Pastor Chaolong Kao specially flew to San Francisco Theological Seminary to attend the graduation ceremony. In July 1972, Dr. Lai’s fiancée, Jane Hatsuko Ueno (a third-generation Japanese-American from Hawaii), and he held their wedding ceremony at FPCLA, officiated by Pastor Kao — the first wedding held after the establishment of the Los Angeles Presbyterian Church.
After that, Dr. Lai disappeared from the Taiwanese church community. He explained that theological education taught him that after a pastor hands over pastoral work to a successor, it is best not to continue attending that church, as it increases pressure on the successor. He also cited his dream of Taiwanese independence and missionary work in China — matters with “untold difficulties” during the turbulent political era.
From “Theology of Hope” to “Theology of Revolution”
The period from 1970 to 1972 was described as “the most tumultuous and terrifying time for Taiwan.” In 1970, the April 24 incident saw Peter Huang shoot at Chingkuo Chiang. In 1971, Taiwan was expelled from the UN. Nixon’s visit to China in February 1972 further worsened Taiwan’s situation.
Inspired by Nixon’s engagement with the CCP, Dr Lai believed the Taiwanese people must study the CCP to learn how to overthrow the KMT. He discovered that Mao Zedong had written articles in 1928 and 1936 supporting Taiwanese independence, and had broadcast support for Taiwanese independence from Yan’an after the February 28 Incident.
Trade with China: “Little Asia Imports”
Dr. Lai established an import company called “Little Asia Imports” (LAImports), borrowing nearly HK$20,000 from friends and family plus his own savings, to procure Chinese handicrafts for wholesale in Los Angeles. He planned to use trade as a means to establish connections with the CCP. The first year ran smoothly, but the Red Guards’ rebellion in China during the Cultural Revolution made international trade nearly impossible, and his “China Dream” ended abruptly.
Taiwan Independent Revolution Army (T.I.R.A.)
While managing his trade business, Dr. Lai joined the “Taiwan Independent Revolution Army” (T.I.R.A.), a secret underground organization founded by Su Beng (史明). He practiced shooting at a range near Highway 60 and Rosemead Boulevard every Saturday, and learned about explosives and demolition. He opened a bank account for T.I.R.A. by placing a three-day DBA advertisement in the classified section of the Los Angeles Times.
The effort came to a standstill when his comrade Kenneth Wang graduated and returned to Brazil, leaving Dr. Lai as the only person in T.I.R.A. About a year and a half later, an FBI agent visited him, having obtained his information from the bank. The agent warned him that armed revolutionary activities are not allowed in the U.S. and fall under the category of terrorist violence.
Maytai Companies and Chinese Community Yellow Pages
During the 1970s wave of Taiwanese refugees fleeing to the U.S., Dr. Lai shifted his focus. With his friend Jihsiung Chen (陳吉雄), a pioneer in international color printing in Taiwan, he founded “Maytai Companies” — the first advertising company, Chinese-language translation company, Chinese color printing factory, and Chinese photographic studio for Taiwanese people in Los Angeles.
By 1980, they established the “Chinese Community Yellow Pages” phone directory, which grew from fewer than 200 pages and 3,000 copies in its first year to nearly 3,000 pages and 100,000 copies within a few years. They later published city versions covering the top ten U.S. cities with large Chinese populations, receiving awards from the Yellow Page Publishers Association, including the Annual Achievement Gold Award.
American Business & Industry and the Nixon Connection
The company’s 1984 Los Angeles Olympic Guide Book attracted the attention of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In 1986, the company published “American Business & Industry” in Shanghai with the Shanghai Publishing Bureau. The press conference at the Jinjiang Hotel was attended by U.S. Consul General in Shanghai and then-Secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Committee Zemin Jiang (江澤民). This was reported on CCTV Evening News — the first time in history that a new book’s publication was reported in a national evening news broadcast in China.
The book featured a “Letter to the People of China” signed by former U.S. President Nixon, which made it a reference for Chinese officials during the reform and opening-up period. This led to ASM becoming the officially designated U.S. training program partner of the State Administration of Foreign Experts Affairs (SAFEA), training over 6,000 Chinese government officials and corporate executives from 1988 to 2000.
The 1996 Missile Crisis and Realization About the CCP
By 1996, when Taiwan held its first direct presidential election, the CCP’s reaction — including missile tests over Taiwan — surprised Dr. Lai. He learned that all personnel in the PLA missile unit were very nervous, worried the missiles might fall back onto Taiwan.
After the 1997 handover of Hong Kong, Dr. Lai finally realized: “In the long run, the CCP is more brutal and terrifying than the KMT for the Taiwanese people.” He gradually recognized that China did not have what he wanted — the secret to overthrowing the KMT. The CCP was not as powerful as it seemed; it was primarily the internal corruption within the KMT that pushed it to the brink.
SIAS College and “Fisherman’s Hall”
Dr. Lai shifted from government training to education, assisting his friend Chen in founding SIAS College (西亞斯學院) in Zhengzhou, Henan. He spent years commuting between Beijing and Zhengzhou, helping develop foreign resources, international student programs, and student clubs (which expanded from fewer than 20 to nearly 200 types).
He also played a key role in establishing “Fisherman’s Hall Christian Church” near SIAS College to serve the 150-180 foreign teachers hired annually. Over twenty years, the church grew from a small chapel serving foreign teachers into a magnificent seven-story building with 40 clergy and staff — far beyond his expectations.
Letting Go: COVID and the End of an Era
In mid-December 2019, Dr. Lai returned to Los Angeles from Beijing and did not return. COVID-19 led to flight suspensions lasting two to three years. During this time, he reassessed the changes in both the U.S. and China, including tightening control over universities and intensifying surveillance of Taiwanese people in China. He officially informed SIAS that he would not be going back.
By 2025, the number of foreign teachers at SIAS had dropped from 150-200 to fewer than 40-50. The party committee at SIAS had expanded from four stationed personnel to 102 party branches covering faculty and students. The U.S.-China relationship had shifted from “quasi-allies” fifty years ago to “quasi-enemies” today.
Sixty Years in America
As Dr. Lai approached completing sixty years in America, he reflected on what he called a “pendulum effect” — sixty years ago, San Francisco was in the midst of a leftist cultural revolution; in 2025, under Trump 2.0, the “MAGA wave” seemed to be resurfacing. He noted that as a passionate youth, he may not have been “far left,” but was not far from being “New Left” — the most popular phrase being “Don’t trust anyone over 30.” Now in his eighties, he found himself supporting MAGA, leaning toward the center-right.

“After careful reflection and humble introspection through prayer, I realize that this dream has not been the one I initially had. I ultimately recognize that in my life, there has always been a dream, and this dream has been realized, but it is not the same dream I started with. God’s arrangements are truly marvelous!”

Postscript: Echoes of History
The Postscript positions Dr. Lai’s dissertation as a prophetic document whose insights remain relevant fifty years later. The issues discussed — Taiwanese identity, political dilemmas, and the pursuit of hope — continue to resonate in contemporary Taiwanese society.
Echoes of History: The Shaping of Taiwanese Identity
The Postscript emphasizes that the dissertation laid the foundation for understanding the unique and complex identity of the Taiwanese people. Through colonial rule by the Dutch, Spanish, Ming and Qing dynasties, and the Japanese government, Taiwan’s history has always been closely linked to foreign influence. Japanese colonial rule (1895–1945) inadvertently contributed to “National Unity” among the Taiwanese people by severing connections with mainland China and improving living standards.
The 228 Incident (1947), estimated to have caused 15,000 to 25,000 deaths, “completely destroyed the Taiwanese people’s illusions about their ‘motherland’ and became a distant cause of the Taiwanese independence movement.” The subsequent martial law and systematic oppression, while consolidating KMT rule, inadvertently strengthened the shared identity of the Taiwanese people and drove many young individuals abroad.
From Exile to Democracy: The “Quiet Revolution”
The Postscript traces Taiwan’s democratization from the 1970s to the present: the Kaohsiung Incident (1979), the establishment of the Democratic Progressive Party (1986), the lifting of martial law (1987), the Wild Lily Movement (1990), the first direct presidential election (1996), and the completion of three transfers of power.
The “Quiet Revolution” nature of Taiwan’s democratization lies in its avoidance of large-scale bloodshed — a lesson drawn from the bloody experiences of the 228 Incident and the Kaohsiung Incident. In the eyes of believers, this peaceful transformation is a manifestation of “God’s grace.”
In 2021, the Economist Intelligence Unit ranked Taiwan eighth in its democracy index, the highest among countries outside the Western world.
A Community of Hope: Christian Faith in Times of Crisis
The Postscript concludes that the Formosan Presbyterian Church in Los Angeles was not merely a religious space but a “Mission of Identity” — providing a foundation of hope for “lost” Taiwanese, preserving and cultivating a unique Taiwanese identity abroad, and providing a platform for the Taiwanese language, culture, and shared experiences.

“This sense of ‘hope’ in Christian faith is not only an ultimate concern but also a practical force that transforms individual suffering under authoritarianism into a commitment to social change, providing a deep moral and spiritual foundation for the ‘Quiet Revolution.‘”

Conclusion: Lessons from History and the Sustainability of Democracy
Dr. Lai’s dissertation, written in 1971, is described as “not only a profound depiction of the Taiwanese people’s struggles at that time but also a prophecy for future transformation.” The journey from Taiwan’s authoritarian oppression beginning in 1945 to today’s thriving democracy is widely praised by the international community as a peaceful “Quiet Revolution” — which can also be viewed as “God’s grace.”

“Learning from history is not merely a retrospective endeavor; it is about continuously constructing a more just and free Taiwanese society, carrying on the mission embodied in ‘Toward a Community of Hope,’ and allowing the light of hope to continue shining on this land.”

Contributions and Legacy

Co-founded FPCLA (1970) — First Taiwanese church in North America, under UPCUSA/PC(USA) system
Authored Toward A Community of Hope (1971) — Foundational dissertation on Taiwanese immigrant church formation, reprinted 2025
Theological vision — Articulated church as both ethnic refuge and public mission community; “hopeful community” theology
Cross-generational reference — 2025 republication linked to NTPC, PCT, and broader Taiwanese church heritage
Seminarian mentor — Taught at TTCS where future leaders including Rev. Chaolong Kao were students

people/alexander-macdonald.title: 馬偕博士 (George Leslie Macdonald)
people/alexander-macdonald.content:
馬偕博士 (George Leslie Macdonald)
George Leslie Macdonald (馬偕, 1838–1901), commonly known in Chinese as 馬偕博士 (Dr. Maxwell), was a Canadian Presbyterian missionary, medical doctor, evangelist, and educator who spent the last 29 years of his life in northern Taiwan, profoundly shaping its religious, educational, and medical landscape.
Identity Snapshot

Full name: George Leslie Macdonald (馬偕)
Born: September 21, 1838, Tullydonnell, Ontario, Canada
Died: June 2, 1901, Tamsui, Taiwan (aged 62)
Education: Roxbury Latin School; Toronto University (MD); Toronto Missionary College
Marriage: Married Henrietta Elizabeth Runnels in 1872; they had one daughter, Emily
Role: Presbyterian medical missionary, evangelist, educator, physician
Mission field: Northern Taiwan (1872–1901)
Known as: 馬偕 (Ma Kai) in Chinese; 馬偕博士 (Dr. Maxwell) by the Taiwanese people
Legacy: Founded the Presbyterian Church in Northern Taiwan, 偕醫學堂 (Ochong Medical School), and the Tamsui Theological College (now STM Taiwan)

Life and Mission
Arrival in Taiwan
George Leslie Macdonald arrived in Tamsui (淡水), northern Taiwan, on August 23, 1872, after studying theology and medicine in Canada and the United States. He was ordained by the Canadian Presbyterian Church and dispatched as a missionary to Taiwan. At age 34, he began his work in a region that was largely unfamiliar to Westerners.
Medical Work
Macdonald established the first Western medicine clinic in northern Taiwan, providing free medical care to the local population. He treated patients from all social backgrounds, often traveling on foot or by horse to reach remote villages. His medical work was instrumental in gaining the trust of the local community and served as a gateway for his evangelistic efforts.
Educational Contributions
His educational legacy is perhaps his most enduring contribution:

偕醫學堂 (Ochong Medical School, 1880): Founded the first modern medical school in northern Taiwan, training local physicians in Western medicine. The school later became part of the National Taiwan University system.
Tamsui Theological College (1881): Established to train Taiwanese pastors and evangelists, ensuring the sustainability of the church. This institution evolved into the current STM Taiwan (聖約翰大學 / Taiwan Theological College and Seminary).
Girls’ Education: Macdonald was a pioneer in advocating for girls’ education in 19th-century Taiwan, establishing schools for girls at a time when this was highly unconventional.

Evangelism
Macdonald walked an estimated 87,500 kilometers across northern Taiwan during his 29-year mission. He:

Established over 60 churches across northern Taiwan
Baptized more than 1,700 converts
Trained and ordained numerous Taiwanese pastors who continued his work after his death
Used the local language (Hokkien) in his preaching, learning it within months of arrival

Language and Cultural Work
Macdonald developed a romanization system for the Hokkien language (known as the “Macdonald system” or 馬唐字) to facilitate Bible translation and local preaching. He also wrote a Hokkien dictionary and grammar, contributing to linguistic scholarship.
Death and Legacy
馬偕博士 died on June 2, 1901, in Tamsui, Taiwan, from a leg infection that he contracted while visiting a patient in a remote area. Despite his deteriorating health, he continued his work until his final days. He was buried in the church cemetery in Tamsui, where his grave remains a historical site.
His death deeply affected the Taiwanese Christian community. According to historical accounts, thousands of Taiwanese people — both Christian and non-Christian — mourned his passing, testifying to the depth of his impact on the region.
Institutions Carrying His Legacy

偕醫中學 (Ochong Teachers College): Now part of the National Taiwan University system
STM Taiwan (台灣神學院): Direct descendant of the Tamsui Theological College he founded
馬偕紀念醫院 (Mackay Memorial Hospital): One of Taiwan’s largest hospital networks, named in his honor
馬偕紀念醫院宜蘭分院: Branch hospital continuing his medical mission
真理大學 (Tunghais University): Has connections to his educational legacy

Commemoration
馬偕博士’s 150th anniversary of missionary work in Taiwan was commemorated in 2022, including special worship services such as the 馬偕博士台灣宣教150週年紀念主日 hosted by Good Shepherd Taiwanese Presbyterian Church on March 6, 2022.
His legacy continues through the many institutions he founded, including STM Taiwan (where Rev. Ming Yuan Hsu studied), the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan, and Mackay Memorial Hospital.

people/anne-shih.title: Anne Shih (施劉秀枝)
people/anne-shih.content:
Anne Shih (施劉秀枝)
Anne Shih (施劉秀枝) is a Taiwanese American arts leader and community volunteer. She has served as Board Chairwoman of the Bowers Museum (寶爾博物館) since 2010, and was re-elected through 2018. She was honored with the Ellis Island Medal of Honor in May 2017.
Identity Snapshot

English: Anne Shih
Chinese: 施劉秀枝
Born: 1946, Minxiong Township, Chiayi County, Taiwan
Immigrated to US: 1978 with husband 施隆盛 and two children
Residences: New Jersey (1978), Huntington Beach (1980)
Role: Board Chairwoman, Bowers Museum (2010–2018)
Geography: Orange County, California
Husband: 施隆盛 (Shi Longsheng), family ran 嘉益汽水廠 (Jiayi Soda Factory) in Chiayi

Early Life in Taiwan
Anne Shih was born in 1946 in Minxiong Township, Chiayi County, Taiwan. Her family ran a cloth and tailor shop. Her father was often away on business trips, teaching her how to interact and speak with people. Every year before Chinese New Year, her mother would send her out to collect debts from customers — a common practice since rural residents saved money by buying fabric, having it tailored, and sometimes paying later.
Her older siblings all studied hard, went to good schools (嘉中, 嘉女), and entered university. Anne only attended 大林中學 for middle school, then passed the exam for 銘傳商專 (Ming Chuan Commercial College).
Immigration to the US
In 1978, Anne married 施隆盛 (Shi Longsheng) and immigrated to the United States with two children. They first lived in New Jersey, then moved to Huntington Beach in 1980. After the children became independent, Anne began volunteering at the Bowers Museum in 1992.
The Soda Factory Anecdote
Anne’s husband’s family ran the 嘉益汽水廠 (Jiayi Soda Factory) in Chiayi. A memorable story from her youth involves a college student named 施隆盛 who delivered a dozen bottles of lemonade to her home. He specifically requested that the empty bottles be returned — not because he was cheap, but because the bottles themselves were valuable. When he really did come to collect the bottles a few days later, he explained: “My family runs a soda factory in Chiayi. The soda isn’t valuable, but the bottles are.”
Bowers Museum
Volunteer and Board Service
Anne began volunteering at the Bowers Museum (寶爾博物館) in 1992. She joined the museum board in 1996 and created the Junior Ambassador program, introducing high school students to art and culture.
In 2005, she was elected Vice Chairwoman. In 2009, she was selected as the museum’s outstanding alumna (銘傳大學). In 2010, she was elected Board Chairwoman and re-elected through terms into 2016–2018.
Major Exhibitions
Anne Shih was credited with initiating many rare exhibitions from Taiwan, Tibet, and China. Notable exhibitions include:

Ancient Egyptian animal mummies
Silk Road exhibitions
Tibet exhibitions
Beijing Palace Museum loans
Terracotta warriors (秦朝兵馬俑)
Qing dynasty jade collections (from 鴻禧美術館)

Peter Keller, the museum’s director since 1991, specialized in gems. In 1991, he wanted to hold a world-class jade exhibition and made two trips to Taiwan empty-handed. He met the still-shy volunteer Anne inside the museum and jokingly asked her to help organize a jade exhibition. To Anne’s surprise, she went to Taipei and successfully borrowed a series of fine Qing dynasty jade pieces from private collectors (鴻禧美術館).
Museum Operations
The Bowers Museum has an annual budget of ~$4.5 million. The Santa Ana city government provides $1.5 million, ticket revenue is ~$750,000, and the rest must be raised by board members through networking and annual fundraising banquets.
Asian/Chinese visitors make up only 5% of the museum’s visitors. The James-Irvine Foundation donated $1.2 million to promote multiculturalism, with one program being to train Chinese-speaking docents. Anne hopes more Chinese Americans will join the volunteer lineup.
The museum’s security staff is divided into three shifts, totaling 65 people. The museum hallways can be rented for events, and artists are invited annually to create works that are submitted to charity auctions.
Over 20 years, the museum has hosted 58 special exhibitions, only 8 of which were China-related. But every time, Anne found a way to raise $1-2 million to prepare them.
Personal Life
Anne is nearly 70 years old at the time of the profile, and shows no signs of fatigue. She is a breast cancer survivor and康复 (rehabilitation) warrior. She loves cooking and is confident in her skills, preparing dinner for her husband every day after 5 PM.
Awards and Recognition

Ellis Island Medal of Honor (May 2017)
Over 10 major awards for her service
One award was named after her: the “Anne Shih Service Award”
銘傳大學 outstanding alumna (2009)
Board chair since 2010, re-elected through 2018

people/bob-j-wu.title: Bob J. Wu (吳瑞椿)
people/bob-j-wu.content:
Bob J. Wu (吳瑞椿)
Bob J. Wu, MD, FACS (吳瑞椿) is a Taiwanese American general surgeon serving the communities around Monterey Park and Rowland Heights, California. He is known for his minimally invasive surgical techniques and his ability to serve the Taiwanese American immigrant community with cultural understanding.
Identity Snapshot

English: Bob J. Wu, MD, FACS
Chinese: 吳瑞椿
Born: Taipei, Taiwan
Lived in Taiwan: First 8 years of life
Immigrated to US: Age 8, California
Education: UCLA (undergraduate); Loma Linda School of Medicine
Specialty: General surgery, minimally invasive surgery
Geography: Monterey Park / Rowland Heights, California
Languages: Mandarin, Taiwanese, Cantonese, Spanish, English
Credentials: FACS (Fellow of the American College of Surgeons)

Early Life
Wu was born in Taipei, Taiwan, and lived there for the first 8 years of his life. As a child, he was content living in the major urban center of Taipei. His father had aspirations for a new possibility — life somewhere with more open spaces, green lawns, swimming pools, and an educational system where children could learn and expand their horizons more freely, rather than face grueling hours of after-school tutoring 6 days a week.
Moving to California was the fulfillment of all these things. Being the youngest member of the family, Wu was the biggest immediate beneficiary of the bold move. He was able to learn English and catch up academically in about 2 years.
Cultural Transition
Transitioning to a new culture was not completely smooth-sailing for Wu. On one hand, he was acutely aware of the sacrifices his parents sustained to make the American dream come true. They had given up stable and well-paying careers to become new immigrants with little job or financial security. On the other hand, during his crucial formative teenage years, he was fortunate to have a church community who sincerely accepted him for who he was.
Being a youth group leader cultivated confidence and allowed him to discover skills and talents he would otherwise not have developed, eventually earning the respect of his peers even in high school. He has always loved music and sports, but even in high school he realized his strongest suit was in science and medicine. Surprisingly, he also did well in Spanish, acquiring his third language.
Education
Knowing education would be his key to success and being aware of the sacrifices his family had made, Wu did not take his grades lightly. He worked hard to ensure a perfect GPA through high school and was fortunate to receive the Regent’s scholarship, which covered his fees through all 4 years of UCLA.
At UCLA, he briefly considered the humanities but realized his strength had always been in science and medicine. He took the unusual route of being a Spanish major, knowing that being fluent in a third language would always be useful, whether he became a doctor, missionary, or even staying in Southern California.
Medical Training
Wu attended Loma Linda School of Medicine, where he was inspired by the school’s motto and mission to “carry on the teaching and healing ministry of Jesus Christ.” The altruistic mission of the school was what inspired him to become a surgeon — a person with immediate life-saving skills that transcend any language barrier and are needed all over the world, especially in underprivileged places.
His training path included:

4 years in medical school
5 years in residency
1 year in fellowship

Along the way, he was blessed to find his soul mate, a wife who shared all of his deepest values, also being an Asian American and a physician herself.
Practice
For the last 5 years (at time of profile), Wu has worked as a general surgeon serving the communities around Monterey Park and Rowland Heights — the exact same neighborhoods where he began his life in the US.
In serving patients, he uses Mandarin, Taiwanese, Cantonese, and even Spanish more than English. Many of his patients are first-generation Taiwanese American immigrants just like his parents, and not infrequently, some of them even know them personally.
Minimally Invasive Surgery
Wu is known for his expertise in minimally invasive surgical techniques. This approach uses 1 to 3 small incisions, performed through a television monitor, as opposed to traditional surgery’s large incisions. The wounds are significantly smaller, and patients recover more quickly.
Personal American Dream
Wu’s personal American dream has come full circle. He works in the same neighborhoods where he grew up, serving the same community that helped him. Though his dreams of being a missionary surgeon going to far-off places have yet to be fulfilled, there is satisfaction in knowing that his skills, training, and languages are being used to their full extent, serving a community with trusted surgical care along with cultural understanding that few others can provide.

Dr. Charles C.L. Kao (Chaolong Kao, 高昭龍) was the organizing minister of the Formosan Presbyterian Church in Los Angeles (FPCLA), called by the Presbytery of Los Angeles Southwest in September 1971 on behalf of the Formosan congregation.

He was a native Formosan, former Assistant Professor at Tainan Theological College, and before accepting the call was a Visiting Scholar at Harvard University.

people/franklin-ping-cheng.title: Franklin Ping Cheng (程炳成)
people/franklin-ping-cheng.content:
Franklin Ping Cheng (程炳成)
Franklin Ping Cheng served as President of the Taiwanese American Historical Society (TAHS) from 2014 to 2017, succeeding founding president Charles Yang (楊嘉猷) who stepped aside due to health reasons. He previously served one year as vice-president before his election.
Identity Snapshot

English: Franklin Ping Cheng
Chinese: 程炳成
Role: President, Taiwanese American Historical Society (2014–2017)
Organizations: Taiwanese American Historical Society (TAHS)
Era: 2014–2017 (TAHS presidency); 2017 publication year

Overview
Franklin Ping Cheng assumed the TAHS presidency in 2014 after serving one year as the Society’s vice-president. The term was originally intended to be three years. He took on the role at a pivotal moment: founding president Charles Yang (楊嘉猷) had stepped aside due to physical health conditions, including two major surgeries, and recovered within a year — but the Society needed steady leadership in the interim.
Under his presidency, the Society emphasized several key initiatives:

Website development: Strengthened the Society’s online presence at www.TAhistory.org
Senior member interviews: Prioritized recording oral histories from senior community members before memory loss could erase their stories
Lectures and forums: Organized community educational programming
Video outreach: Published content on YouTube and the Society’s website
2017 yearbook: Supported founding president Yang’s vision to publish a special yearbook introducing community profiles — the 台美菁英錄 (Taiwanese American Elite Record) — which introduced four prominent TA entrepreneurs and outstanding second-generation leaders

In his November 2017 會長謝詞 (President’s Gratitude) in the yearbook, Franklin expressed hope that future publications could include many more community members, and invited recommendations for future profile subjects. He also noted his satisfaction that Yang was well enough to lead the Society again the following year to complete his term.
The 2017 yearbook was made possible with special sponsorship from TECO (僑委會 — Overseas Community Development Foundation), acknowledged in the publication.
Source Notes and Confidence

people/guo-yingyan.content:
Guo Yingyan (郭應言)
Guo Yingyan (郭應言, Rev. Guo / 郭牧師) was a pastor connected with the early development of Irvine Taiwanese Presbyterian Church (爾灣台灣基督長老教會 (PCT)). The church’s official history identifies him as a pastor who served ITPC after the departure of the founding-stage pastor 鄭泉聲牧師.
ITPC Role
The ITPC history document states that after 鄭泉聲牧師 returned to Japan, the congregation invited nearby pastors to help with pastoral care until 郭應言牧師 was called approximately a year later. It describes 郭應言牧師 as previously serving at a “House of Christ” church context and notes that he resigned after about one year because he was not accustomed to the Presbyterian church system.
Historical Significance
郭應言牧師’s brief service reflects the transitional period between ITPC’s founding independence and its later full-time pastoral stability. His tenure sits in the late-1990s period when the congregation was still worshiping at Creekside Fellowship Church and seeking durable pastoral leadership.

people/hsu-hsin-hung.title: Hsu Hsin-hung (徐新宏)
people/hsu-hsin-hung.content:
Hsu Hsin-hung (徐新宏)
Hsu Hsin-hung (徐新宏, born 1947) is a Taiwanese American scientist and entrepreneur who serves as Chairman and CEO of the Chia Ho Enterprise Group (佳和企業集團) in California. He holds a Ph.D. and founded J.H. Biotech, Inc. in 1987, building a multinational enterprise focused on organic agriculture, biotechnology, and health products.
Identity Snapshot

English: Hsu Hsin-hung
Chinese: 徐新宏
Born: 1947, Tongxiao (通宵鎮), Miaoli County, Taiwan (February 28 — the day of the 228 Incident)
Spouse: 陳麗華 (Chen Li-hua)
Education: B.S. Agricultural Chemistry, National Chung Hsing University (中興大學), 1967; M.S. and Ph.D. (U.S.)
Key role: Chairman and CEO, Chia Ho Enterprise Group
Founded: J.H. Biotech, Inc. (1987), Ventura County, California
Organizations: Chia Ho Enterprise Group; J.H. Biotech; 佳和生物科技公司

Early Life
Hsu Hsin-hung was born in 1947 in Tongxiao Township, Miaoli County, Taiwan — the same year the 228 Incident occurred, an event that profoundly shaped Taiwanese history. His family lived in rural areas for generations and worked as farmers. His father had limited formal education, and his mother was illiterate, yet they placed enormous value on education and did everything within their means to raise their children.
Because of his farming background, Hsu helped his parents with farm work from a young age — herding cattle, raising pigs, plowing, transplanting rice, and harvesting. He was skilled at all farm labor. He later described himself as carrying the “Taiwanese water buffalo” spirit: honest, simple, hardworking, and resilient. This close connection to the land instilled in him a deep sense of gratitude and love for his homeland (“吃果子拜樹頭、愛鄉愛土” — when you eat fruit, you honor the tree that bore it).
Education and Mentorship
In high school, Hsu’s favorite subjects were chemistry and biology, which led him to choose the Agricultural Chemistry Department at National Chung Hsing University (中興大學) in 1967.
At Chung Hsing University, Hsu encountered Professor Sun Chi-ning (孫志寧), who profoundly influenced his approach to both work and scholarship. Hsu recounts an incident that became a guiding principle for his entire life:
During a lab experiment, Hsu accidentally knocked over an entire rack of dozens of test tubes from the oven. Test tubes of good quality had to be imported, and he was terrified. Professor Sun said nothing at first — she simply picked up a broom and silently swept up the glass shards. When she was done, she said: “Making mistakes is inevitable. The only way to never make a mistake is to never do anything. Don’t be afraid of making mistakes — be proactive and do it.”
This simple sentence shaped Hsu’s entire philosophy. He later called it his “practical philosophy” (力行哲學): plan carefully, then act. Many people stop at the planning stage because they fear failure or loss. True progress comes from execution, learning from errors, and moving forward.
This became the cornerstone of his later entrepreneurial success.
Career
J.H. Biotech
In 1987, Hsu resigned from his position in Utah and founded J.H. Biotech, Inc. (佳和生物科技公司) in his home state. In 1988, he relocated to Ventura County, California, where, with the help of his wife, he built the company over many years into a multinational enterprise with branches and subsidiaries spread across several countries.
The enterprise’s business lines include:

Organic (microbial) pesticides
Organic (microbial) fertilizers
Biological (animal) feed additives
Human health food ingredients (R&D, production, and sales)

These all connected directly to his university studies and research. Hsu described his founding motivation as: “Considering the health and safety of users and consumers, and focusing on reducing pollution. We aimed to establish a different model in the agricultural production sector and work toward the goal of a ‘green planet.‘”
Chia Ho Enterprise Group
Over years of dedicated work, Hsu built a diversified enterprise group with operations spanning multiple countries. He serves as both Chairman and CEO, overseeing the group’s strategic direction across all business lines.
Taiwan Identity and Community Engagement
Hsu Hsin-hung distinguishes himself from many other Taiwanese American entrepreneurs through his strong Taiwan identity and advocacy. He has been vocal about his views on cross-strait relations, even before President Chen Shui-bian’s “one side, one state” (一邊一國) statement.
In 2002–2003, at his first Overseas Community Affairs Council (僑務委員會) meeting, Hsu noticed that even Chairman Chang Fu-mei (張富美) and others constantly used the terms “兩岸” (cross-strait) and “大陸” (mainland). He publicly raised concerns about this terminology and privately advised the Chairman to use “兩國” (two countries) instead, noting that “China” should be called “China,” not “mainland.”
Hsu was particularly concerned that even green-leaning media and commentators sometimes casually used terms like “大陸” and “兩岸” without realizing, in his view, that they had been “poisoned” by unificationist discourse. He emphasized that he had been attentive to this issue long before it became a mainstream debate.
Honors and Recognition

2010: Elected as the 14th Distinguished Alumnus of National Chung Hsing University (中興大學第14屆傑出校友)
In his acceptance speech, Hsu recalled his graduate experience with Professor Sun and described his commitment to green product development and environmental protection

Personal Philosophy
Hsu’s life philosophy can be summarized by the “water buffalo spirit” (台灣水牛精神): hard work, perseverance, and humility. His approach to business and life is encapsulated in Professor Sun’s teaching: plan well, act decisively, learn from mistakes, and keep going.
He is known for his strong Taiwan identity, his commitment to giving back to both his adopted country (America) and his homeland (Taiwan), and his belief that success should benefit farmers, consumers, and the environment.

people/huang-gen-shen.title: Huang Gen-shen (黃根深)
people/huang-gen-shen.content:
Huang Gen-shen (黃根深)
Identity Snapshot

Born: ~1940s, Wanhua Post Station, Taipei, Taiwan
Era: First-generation Taiwanese American
Geography: Memphis (Tennessee) → Los Angeles, California
Core roles: Art teacher, UFAI/台獨聯盟 founding member (51-year activist), political artist, illustrator

Overview

黃根深 (Huang Gen-shen) was an art teacher and the only artist among the founding members of the United Formosans for Independence (UFI) and later the United Formosans for Independence (UFAI)
He graduated from the Department of Fine Arts at Taiwan Normal College (now National Taiwan Normal University) and studied art in the United States at the University of Iowa and UCLA
In 1965, he arrived in the US in September; his father died in December. He sent $2,000 (his entire student bond) back to Taiwan, then worked in Los Angeles while taking classes at UCLA
He joined the UFI (later UFAI) in 1966 after being introduced by Lai Wen-xiong (賴文雄), a lifelong friend
He served as secretary and periodical publisher for the UFI’s first long-lived publication, Formosan Gram《福爾摩沙通訊》, which began monthly publication in 1966
He designed the UFAI logo (a triangle over a circle), illustrations, and covers for UFAI publications including the long-running magazine Wang Chun Feng《望春風》
He donated his artwork for UFAI fundraising auctions; some buyers did not realize the artist was him — his paintings hung in fellow activists’ living rooms
He remained an active member through decades of internal struggles and crises, including the 424 Chiang Ching-kuo assassination attempt, and was still a Central Committee member two years before the 2017 publication
He participated in all major Taiwanese American organizations: FAPA, 全美台灣人權會, 同鄉會, and helped revive the Western Taiwan Summer Camp after it had been dormant for over ten years
His wife was a 228 victim’s relative (王平水’s third daughter); their marriage would have been opposed by his family in Taiwan due to her father’s death in the 228 massacre
He was placed on the Kuomintang blacklist after a “snitch” (抓耙仔) was exposed in their organization, and his family in Taiwan was subsequently harassed
After the blacklist was lifted, he rarely returned to Taiwan, saying Taiwan had changed so fast it felt like “another country” — lost its “Taiwan flavor”
In 2017, he participated in the Overseas 228 Survivors’ Family Return to Taiwan program, organized by the Overseas Chinese Affairs Council (僑委會)
He expressed concern about Taiwan’s political future, urging the government to consider allowing people who wish to return to China to do so — warning that Taiwan could become a bargaining chip between great powers
He was described as the hardest-working member at UFAI activities: providing artwork for charity auctions, assisting Taiwanese American organizations with events, drawing cartoons and designing covers for their publications

people/jack-j-chen.title: Jack J. Chen (陳宏傑)
people/jack-j-chen.content:
Jack J. Chen (陳宏傑)
Jack J. Chen, PharmD is a Taiwanese American clinical pharmacist and researcher, double board-certified in Pharmacotherapy and Geriatric Pharmacy Practice. He is a Full Professor and Founding Chair of the Department of Pharmacy Practice at Marshall B. Ketchum University College of Pharmacy.
Identity Snapshot

English: Jack J. Chen
Chinese: 陳宏傑
Born: South Bend, Indiana
Raised: Southern California
Education: BA Animal Physiology, UC San Diego (1989); BS Pharmacy, MCPHS (1993); PharmD, University of Utah (1995)
Specialty: Clinical neurology, neurology pharmacotherapy, movement disorders
Current role: Full Professor, Founding Chair, Dept of Pharmacy Practice, Marshall B. Ketchum University COP
Geography: Southern California
Credentials: FCPhA, FASCP, FCCP
Family: Married with twin daughters

Education and Training

BA Animal Physiology, UC San Diego (1989)
BS Pharmacy, Massachusetts College of Pharmacy and Health Sciences (1993)
PharmD, University of Utah (1995)
Specialty Pharmacy Residency (Internal Medicine), Rush University Medical Center, Chicago (1996)
Clinical Neurology Preceptorship, Movement Disorders Center, Loma Linda University (2003–2005)

Career
Huntington Memorial Hospital (1996–2000)
Clinical pharmacist at Huntington Memorial Hospital, Pasadena, CA.
Western University of Health Sciences (2000–2005)
Assistant Professor at the Western University of Health Sciences School of Pharmacy, where he developed and taught the PharmD neurology therapeutics courses and served as Director of Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experiences and faculty advisor to the American Pharmacists Association (APhA) Academy of Student Pharmacists.
Loma Linda University (2005–2014)
Associate Professor at Loma Linda University (LLU) School of Pharmacy, where he was instrumental in developing and teaching the PharmD neurology therapeutics course. He also served as the Director of Scholarly Activities to foster a departmental culture of scholarship. In 2013, he received an award as LLU School of Pharmacy Teacher of the Year. At LLU, Dr. Chen also established, obtained funding, and co-directed an interprofessional, clinical neurology movement disorders preceptorship program within the Department of Neurology.
Marshall B. Ketchum University (2014–present)
Full Professor and Founding Chair for the Department of Pharmacy Practice at the Marshall B. Ketchum University College of Pharmacy.
Research and Publications
Dr. Chen maintains a sustained record of scholarship in the field of Neurology Pharmacotherapy with an emphasis in Movement Disorders. He is an author on 160 peer-reviewed manuscripts, book chapters, and abstracts.
His research focus includes:

Neurology pharmacotherapy
Movement disorders
Clinical neurology
Geriatric pharmacy practice

Awards and Honors

ASHP Drug Therapy Research Award (1999) — American Society of Health-System Pharmacist
CPNP Original Research Award (2014, 2017) — College of Psychiatric and Neurologic Pharmacists
Drug Topics Hospital Pharmacist of the Year (2000)
CPhA Distinguished Young Pharmacist of the Year (2002)
SGVSHP Pharmacist of the Year (2002)
LLU School of Pharmacy Teacher of the Year (2013)
Fellow of the CPhA (FCPhA)

Professional Service

American Academy of Neurology (AAN) delegate to the United States Pharmacopeial Convention
Founding member of the AAN Neurologic Therapies Workgroup
Committee chair within national and state professional organizations including:

American Colleges of Clinical Pharmacy (ACCP) Central Nervous System Practice and Research Network (2012-2013)
American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy New Pharmacy Faculty Research Awards Program Review Team (2010)
California Pharmacist Association (CPhA) Educational Foundation Advisory Committee (2000–2002)
California Society of Health-System Pharmacist Seminar Poster Session (1999–2005)
Member-at-Large for the APhA Academy of Pharmacy Practice and Management Hospital & Institutional Practice Section (2000–2002)


Served as committee chair within professional organizations including the San Gabriel Valley Society of Health-System Pharmacists (SGVSHP; 2002–2003), the Southeast Los Angeles Pharmacists Association (2001–2005), and the Southern California College of Clinical Pharmacy (2004–2006)

people/john-chiang.title: John Chiang (江俊輝)
people/john-chiang.content:
John Chiang (江俊輝)
John Chiang (江俊輝, born 1962) is a Taiwanese American politician who serves as California State Controller, the state’s chief financial officer. He was elected to the office in 2006 at age 45 and has served since. He previously worked as a prosecutor for 12 years.
Identity Snapshot

English: John Chiang
Chinese: 江俊輝
Born: 1962, New York City
Parents: 江牧東 (Mudong Chiang) — Taipei-born chemical engineer, NTU Class of 1950s; 沈吟香 (Yinhsiang Shen) — Tainan-born, studied in Japan, Notre Dame. Mother’s father: 沈榮 (Shen Rong), a respected lawyer who helped the poor.
Siblings: 江宜玲 (Joyce Chiang, 1965–1999) — immigration lawyer, Clinton administration; 江俊德 (Robert Chiang) — physician; 江俊立 (Roger Chiang) — MBA, producer on American Most Wanted
Education: DePaul University (transfer); University of South Florida (Finance); Georgetown University Law Center (J.D.)
Office: California State Controller (elected 2006, 2010); California State Treasurer (2015–present)
Previous role: IRS tax law specialist; attorney for Gray Davis (1999–2003); staff member for Sen. Barbara Boxer; Chief of Staff for CA Board of Equalization Commissioner Brad Sherman
Geography: California (Sacramento / Los Angeles / Washington DC)
Heritage: Second-generation Taiwanese American

Early Life and Education
John Chiang was born in New York City in 1962 to Taiwanese immigrant parents. His father, 江牧東 (Mudong Chiang), was a Taipei-born chemical engineer who graduated from National Taiwan University in the 1950s and earned a PhD in chemical engineering from Cleveland Institute of Technology. His mother, 沈吟香 (Yinhsiang Shen), was from Tainan, studied in Japan, and met his father at the University of Notre Dame. His maternal grandfather, 沈榮 (Shen Rong), was a highly respected lawyer in Tainan who helped the poor — a visit to him left a lasting impression on young John, who decided then he wanted to be a lawyer.
The family moved to a Chicago suburb (about 30 minutes from Chicago) where they were the first Asian American family in the neighborhood. Young John faced racial discrimination: other children excluded him and his siblings, threw stones at their house, wrote insults on walls, and destroyed their mailboxes. When his younger brother Roger was learning to ride a bicycle, older kids beat him up, so John — three or four years older — fought back to protect his siblings, getting labeled a troublemaker by the school. The family also faced cultural isolation: the children’s Taiwanese bento boxes (rice, fish or beef, vegetables) contrasted sharply with other kids’ sandwiches. His mother, a devout Catholic, began attending church regularly hoping to find acceptance and bridge cultural differences. She also actively participated in community activities, earning the respect of local elected officials who would advocate on the family’s behalf.
The family raised four children with strict traditional Chinese values: treat people with sincerity, no hypocrisy, no vanity, no jealousy. The children’s names were chosen so that two start with J (John, Joyce) and two with R (Robert, Roger).
After high school, John earned a full accounting scholarship, attended DePaul University, then transferred to the University of South Florida where he graduated with a finance degree. He then attended Georgetown University Law Center, earning his J.D.
Political Career
Board of Equalization
In 1987, John moved to Southern California to find new opportunities. The IRS had an opening, and he applied and was hired as a tax law specialist for the IRS Los Angeles office. Through his sister Joyce’s internship with Congressman Howard Berman’s Los Angeles office, John met Berman’s staff who recognized his political acumen and encouraged him to consider public service.
John subsequently worked in the offices of several California political leaders — including then-State Controller Gray Davis, Senator Barbara Boxer, and Congressman Mel Levine — as a legal advisor. He eventually became Chief of Staff for California Board of Equalization Los Angeles district commissioner Brad Sherman. When Sherman was elected to Congress in 1997, John was appointed to fill the vacancy.
The California Board of Equalization is the only democratically elected tax agency in the United States. It collects approximately $40–43 billion in annual taxes, accounting for one-third of the state government’s funding. In 1998, John ran for the first time and won with nearly 800,000 votes, becoming the highest-ranking Asian American elected official in California’s executive branch.
State Controller
On January 3, 1999, at age 36, John was sworn in as a member of the California Board of Equalization, representing the 4th district which included Greater Los Angeles and 73 cities.
In November 2006, at age 45, Chiang was elected California State Controller, defeating Republican Tony Strickland with 3,338,081 votes (51%). He became the highest-ranking Taiwanese American in elected executive office in American history. As State Controller, he supervised California’s $1 trillion budget and served as the state’s chief financial officer.
In 2008, Chiang’s political reputation was cemented when he resisted then-Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger’s executive order to cut public employee salaries to reduce the deficit. Schwarzenegger sued, but a California judge rejected the governor’s request for a temporary restraining order. The case was ultimately won by Chiang in California Superior Court. The Los Angeles Times published a special report noting that Chiang’s ability to successfully challenge the governor was due not only to his tax expertise but also to his long-standing involvement with labor organizations.
During his tenure, Chiang also refused to pay legislators’ salaries when the state budget could not be balanced on time — a move that earned widespread praise from constituents.
In 2010, he was re-elected as State Controller. In 2014, his second term ended and he could not run for re-election due to term limits, so he ran for California State Treasurer, winning in 2014 and taking office in 2015.
Community Engagement
Throughout his political career, Chiang has consistently given back to the Taiwanese American community. He served as president of the Taiwanese American Lawyers Association and as a board member of the Los Angeles Taiwan Cultural Center. In 2013, Taiwanese community organizations held a fundraiser in Monterey Park supporting his campaign for State Treasurer. World Federation of Taiwanese Congress President 楊信 (Yang Hsin) praised Chiang’s sincerity and dedication, urging full community support. TACL President 田詒鴻 (Alan Thian), Taiwan Chamber of Commerce President 陳柏宇, and Taiwan Cultural Association Chairman 王梅鳳 all publicly endorsed him.
Chiang also established a political internship program through TACL, opening his office to young Taiwanese Americans for civic engagement experience.
Tragedy: Loss of Sister Joyce
On January 9, 1999 — just one week after John was sworn in as a Board of Equalization member — John’s sister 江宜玲 (Joyce Chiang, born 1965) went missing. Joyce was an immigration lawyer working for the Clinton administration Immigration and Naturalization Service in Washington, DC, living with her younger brother Roger.
John immediately contacted authorities and coordinated the search. The next day, Joyce’s green leather jacket and government work ID were found near Anacostia Park. Four months later, her body was discovered 19 miles from where she disappeared, in the Potomac River. The cause of death could not be determined and no suspects were identified. The case was listed as cold.
In May 2011, after 12 years, Washington Police Chief Cathy Lanier announced the case was solved: Joyce had been murdered. Two suspects were identified but there was insufficient evidence to prosecute. Chief Lanier apologized for investigative errors. John’s brother Roger, who had been searching for answers, had connected with the TV show American Most Wanted host John Walsh and joined the production team to help solve the case.
Joyce had graduated from Smith College (where she was student body president) and Georgetown University Law School, specializing in immigration law. She was known for her vitality, generosity, and commitment to public service. John said his sister was given to him by God, and though she was gone, he would continue the good work she had started.
Political Philosophy
Chiang’s political image was built on a step-by-step effort process and his commitment to the Taiwanese American community. He is known for his fiscal conservatism, transparency, and dedication to serving the public interest. His supporters come from diverse ethnic constituencies — Asian Americans, Latinos, women, Jewish Americans, African Americans — and he has always maintained ties to the Taiwanese American community.
His childhood experience with racial discrimination shaped his worldview. He witnessed how the absence of diverse voices in government led to outdated practices and unjust laws. Inspired by Japanese American congressmen who started from political interns and expanded their influence to broader civil rights issues, he believed that every field — government agencies, industry organizations — needs diverse talent to improve systems.
Source Notes and Confidence

people/jonah-chang.content:
Rev. Jonah Chang (張瑞雄)
Rev. Jonah Chang (張瑞雄) was a former minister of the Presbyterian Church of Formosa who, while serving the United Methodist Church in Fresno, California, led the one-month experimental Formosan church in Los Angeles in August 1970 that catalyzed the permanent Formosan Christian Church / FPCLA.
Identity Snapshot

Primary work page: Toward A Community of Hope (work & sources)
Full text (GitHub): complete extract


English: Rev. Jonah Chang
Chinese: 張瑞雄
Era: 1960s–1970s (documented 1967–1970 experiments)
Geography: Formosa/Taiwan → Fresno, California; ministry impact in Los Angeles
Core roles: Experimental-church leader; Methodist pastor (Fresno); former Presbyterian Church of Formosa minister

Role in FPCLA Origins
August 1970 Experimental Church
From Dr. Albert S. Lai’s 1971 dissertation:

In August 1970, Rev. Jonah Chang started a one-month experimental church to test feasibility of a Formosan congregation in Los Angeles.
First experimental Sunday worship: August 9, 1970 — 22 adults and 11 children attended.
After four Sundays, when Chang returned to Fresno at month’s end, the majority decided to organize a permanent church without a settled pastor and without outside financial support.
Early facility support came via Centenary United Methodist Church and Rev. Peter Chen (Wesley Hall) until the move to Wilshire Crest Presbyterian Church in July 1971.

Taiyou Church (太陽教會) Context
Later republication materials and wiki narrative also associate Chang with an earlier Taiyou Church (太陽教會) experimental effort (c. 1967) using Japanese Methodist facilities — treat as B-tier context pending fuller primary citation in the archive chunks.

people/katherine-huang.title: Katherine Huang (黃愷怡)
people/katherine-huang.content:
Katherine Huang (黃愷怡)
Katherine Kai-Yi Huang (黃愷怡) is a prominent Taiwanese American litigation attorney and founder of the Los Angeles-based law firm of Huang Ybarra Singer & May LLP. She specializes in commercial litigation and has represented clients in high-stakes cases across multiple industries.
Identity Snapshot

English: Katherine Kai-Yi Huang
Chinese: 黃愷怡
Born: Taiwan; immigrated to US at age 5
Education: A.B. Chemistry, Harvard University, summa cum laude (1996); J.D., Yale Law School (2000)
Role: Founding partner, Huang Ybarra Singer & May LLP
Specialty: Commercial litigation
Geography: Los Angeles, California
Languages: Taiwanese, Mandarin, Spanish, English

Education
Huang was born in Taiwan and immigrated to the United States at age 5. She excelled academically:

Harvard University (A.B. Chemistry, summa cum laude, 1996)
Yale Law School (J.D., 2000)
Editor, The Yale Symposium on Law & Technology

Her academic achievements were exceptional, particularly as someone who arrived in the US as a young child and navigated the American education system.
Career
Law Clerk
After law school, Huang served as a law clerk to Judge Samuel A. Alito, Jr., then on the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. Alito was later elevated to the United States Supreme Court.
Munger Tolles & Olson
Huang joined the nationally recognized firm of Munger Tolles & Olson LLP as a partner, where she handled complex commercial litigation matters.
Huang Ybarra Singer & May LLP
Huang founded her own firm, Huang Ybarra Singer & May LLP, specializing in commercial litigation. The firm handles matters ranging from two-party contract disputes to complex, multi-party litigation across the high-tech, energy, financial and legal services, media and entertainment, and manufacturing sectors.
Notable Cases
TASA Lawsuit (2015)
In 2015, Huang represented the Taiwanese American Seniors Association (TASA) in a dispute with certain former directors who had wrongfully taken the organization’s funds for their own use. After a month-long trial, the court ordered the former directors to return all of the funds to TASA and pay punitive damages. This case was significant for the Taiwanese American community, as it recovered misappropriated funds and held the former directors accountable.
Recognition

Daily Journal’s “Top 20 Under 40” (2015)
Los Angeles Magazine’s Top Women Attorneys of Southern California (2015)
Southern California Super Lawyer (2016-2018)
Rising Star (2009-2011, 2015)

Community Involvement
Huang serves on the board of directors of the Westside Infant-Family Network, an award-winning nonprofit organization that provides mental health therapy to young children and their families.
She is proficient in Taiwanese, Mandarin, and Spanish, and has taught creative writing and language skills to elementary and middle school students.

people/liao-ji-chun.title: Liao Jichun (廖繼春)
people/liao-ji-chun.content:
Liao Jichun (廖繼春)
Liao Jichun (廖繼春, 1902–1976) was a renowned Taiwanese painter, celebrated as one of the pioneering figures of modern Taiwanese art. He served as an art teacher at 台中師範學校 (Taichung Normal School) and was the father of biochemist 廖述宗 (Liao Shu-zong).
Identity Snapshot

English: Liao Jichun
Chinese: 廖繼春
Born: 1902, Taiwan
Died: 1976
Spouse: 林瓊仙 (Lin Qiong-xian)
Children: 8 (including 廖述宗 as third child)
Profession: Painter, art teacher
Geography: Tainan, Taichung, Taiwan
Core roles: Modern Taiwanese painter; 台中師範學校 art teacher

Artistic Career
Liao Jichun was a famous painter whose work became foundational to modern Taiwanese art. He taught art at 台中師範學校 (Taichung Normal School), where he influenced many students during his tenure. His painting style and creative approach had a profound impact on his son, 廖述宗, who later credited his father’s artistic imagination as the source of his own scientific creativity.
Liao was known as a quiet, gentle man whose passion was expressed entirely through painting. He took a laissez-faire approach to raising his children, allowing them the freedom to develop their own talents and interests.
Family Legacy
Liao’s creative spirit and artistic vision extended beyond his own work. His son 廖述宗 described his father’s influence as “无形而深远” (formless but profound), stating: “My creativity and discoveries in science came from his imagination and expression in art.”
The family also ran a stationery shop called “文藝社” (Wenyi She) at home, which served as a cultural gathering place in their community.
