people/liao-shu-zong.title: Liao Shu-zong (廖述宗)
people/liao-shu-zong.content:
Liao Shu-zong (廖述宗)
Liao Shu-zong (廖述宗, 1931–2017) was a renowned biochemist and a founding figure in both international biochemistry and the Taiwanese democratic movement. He was a professor at the University of Chicago’s Ben May Department of Molecular Biology, best known for his discovery that testosterone must be converted by a 5-alpha-reductase enzyme to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) to produce biological effects — a breakthrough that revolutionized the understanding of male hormone action and led to the development of multi-billion-dollar pharmaceuticals.
Identity Snapshot

English: Liao Shu-zong
Chinese: 廖述宗
Born: 1931, Tainan, Taiwan
Died: 2017
Father: 廖繼春 (Liao Jichun), famous Taiwanese painter
Mother: 林瓊仙 (Lin Qiong-xian), from a prominent Fengyuan family, graduated from 彰化高女 (first class)
Spouse: 郭淑卿 (Guo Shu-qing), graduated from Tokyo Jishu Women’s University, later studied at Chicago Jishu Women’s Seminary
Children: 4 daughters — 慈瑛, 慈芬, 慈明, 慈卿
Education: B.S. Agricultural Chemistry, National Taiwan University (1954); Ph.D. Biochemistry, University of Chicago (1961)
Core roles: Biochemist; NATPA founder; democratic movement supporter
Geography: Chicago, Illinois (University of Chicago)

Early Life
Liao Shu-zong was born in 1931 in Tainan, Taiwan. He was the third of eight children (two older brothers, four younger sisters). His father, 廖繼春 (Liao Jichun), was a famous painter. His mother, 林瓊仙 (Lin Qiong-xian), came from a prominent Fengyuan family and was the first graduate of the 2nd class of 彰化高女 (Changhua Girls’ Normal School). She was热心公益 (enthusiastically involved in public welfare) and skilled at matchmaking.
The family ran a stationery shop called “文藝社” (Wenyi She) at home. Liao’s mother also taught art at a school in Tainan. From a young age, Liao helped his mother cook, do household chores, watch the shop, and sell stationery.
His father was a quiet, gentle man whose passion was expressed entirely through painting. He took a laissez-faire approach to his children. Liao later said: “His influence on me was无形而深远 (formless but profound). My creativity and discoveries in science came from his imagination and expression in art.”
Liao had always loved observing living things. He raised many silkwatches, watching them grow, form cocoons, become pupae, and emerge as butterflies. He found life itself wondrous. In 3rd grade, he encountered a Japanese teacher named Hoshikoshi Hajime (星襄一), who often took students to the forest for outdoor classes. This teacher’s influence was formative.
228 Incident
When Liao was in 2nd year of 台中一中 (Taichung First Middle School), the 228 Incident occurred. The bloody massacre haunted him for the rest of his life. He described it as the “blackest page” of his youth.
He witnessed people being arrested and paraded through the streets before execution. He saw a bound-footed old mother desperately chasing a prison cart, unable to catch up — “a scene that made you unable to hold back tears.”
Near Taichung First Middle School was a large field where provincial athletic games were held. During the massacres, the Nationalist military executed people there. When executions were scheduled, the school was forced to stop classes and students were compelled to stand on the field and watch. “It was extremely cruel. Every time I went home, I felt like vomiting.”
Political Shadows
The gloomy era and dark political shadows made Liao a thoughtful young man. As a high school student, he frequently read extracurricular books, pondered the meaning of life, and sympathized with the poor and disadvantaged.
In 1949, Liao graduated from Taichung First Middle School with excellent grades and entered the Agricultural Chemistry Department at National Taiwan University (NTU). He chose it because: “NTU had zoology and botany departments, but no biochemistry department, so I chose agricultural chemistry, which combined both biology and chemistry.”
He also briefly connected with the medical school. During his sophomore summer, he took the transfer exam and ranked first in the medical school. But after attending only 3 days, he dropped out. A zoology professor had asked students to memorize over 200 bone names in 3 days. Liao felt his brain shouldn’t be filled only with rote memorization. He returned to agricultural chemistry and never regretted it. “Because I studied agricultural chemistry, my development became even broader.”
Education and PhD
Liao’s excellent performance in the agricultural chemistry department allowed him to serve as a research assistant in Professor He Fanggai’s (何芳陔) lab starting from his junior year, working on wood ear mushroom research.
In 1954, he completed his bachelor’s degree and served as a reserve second lieutenant in the Navy headquarters at Zuoying (左營海軍總部) for one year. After his reserve officer discharge, he returned to NTU’s Agricultural Chemistry Institute for graduate studies.
Under Professor Wu Long-xi (吳龍溪), he independently developed a method of cultivating mushrooms using chemical liquids. This thesis not only earned him his NTU master’s degree but also won him a generous scholarship from the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT), allowing him to begin his study abroad journey in 1956.
Arrival at IIT and Setback
In the fall of 1956, Liao arrived in Chicago with great ambition, hoping to return to Taiwan after a few years with his PhD. He enrolled in the biology department at IIT. The department head, Dr. Hedrick, told him that his cultivated mushrooms were too small to have economic value, so the research plan was canceled. However, the department assigned him to a larger, more famous research group.
The group was working on extracting antibiotics from Lake Michigan water. Antibiotics were highly valued at the time, and if they could extract them from lake water, it would be a major breakthrough. A pilot plant had been built on the shore of Lake Michigan, and Liao was assigned to manage it. But before going, he had to learn the extraction methods in the lab.
Liao tried everything but could not produce the desired results. As days passed, his confidence waned. He prepared to pack up and leave.
He confessed his failure to the department head, but asked to run one more experiment together to understand where things went wrong. Dr. Hedrick agreed. They worked together for three months without results.
Liao then reviewed previous experimental records and discovered the problem: the previous experiments had not measured the pH of the ion-exchange column effluent. In other words, the bacteria were killed by the acidity of the liquid itself, not by antibiotics in the lake water.
The department head was shocked. This meant the entire research plan’s premise was wrong, and the pilot plant had to be closed.
“I didn’t know whether to be happy or sad,” Liao said. “Happy because my experiment was correct — I regained some confidence. Sad because I had just arrived at a new place and had destroyed an entire research program.”
After thinking it over, he decided to leave. But the department head asked him to stay, saying the department was actually grateful for his discovery, since it was better to end early than to invest more capital.
The Chance Visit to UChicago
In the summer of 1957, as Liao was preparing to leave for Ithaca, New York (to enroll at Cornell University under Professor Robert Holley, who had written to recruit him), a friend advised him to visit the University of Chicago before leaving.
On a sunny day, Liao took a train to the Hyde Park campus. He wandered around, admiring the Gothic castles, green lawns, and the echoing bells. He entered the biochemistry building and saw a nameplate outside an office: “Earl Evans, Ph.D.” — the department head. He knocked.
As it happened, Dr. Evans answered the door personally. He not only invited Liao in but sat down to talk and showed him around the lab. Liao was flattered and left happily.
That afternoon at 5 PM, he received a call from Dr. Evans, asking him to return the next day. Confused, Liao went as instructed.
Dr. Evans directed him to the “Ben May” Cancer Research Center to meet Professor Paul Talalay. Liao found Dr. Talalay, who immediately handed him a lab coat and began running experiments together.
They worked until 4 PM. Dr. Talalay asked him to take home some materials to read. Liao was confused — he was supposed to go to Cornell in two days. He explained: “I just visited UChicago, and in two days I’m heading to Cornell for my PhD.”
“What?” Dr. Talalay was stunned. “Didn’t you come here to study? We held a meeting yesterday and discussed your scholarship and research project!”
It turned out they had mistaken his casual visit for a formal enrollment. Liao stayed.
Working with Dr. Charles Huggins
Through Dr. Talalay, Liao was introduced to Dr. Charles Huggins (哈更斯), the 1966 Nobel Prize laureate and “father of chemotherapy.” Dr. Huggins had discovered in 1941 that cancer cells require hormones to grow, and proposed treating prostate cancer by removing male hormones — a treatment that became the global standard. He later applied the same approach to breast cancer with similar success.
In 1950, Dr. Huggins received a donation from Mr. Mermine of Alabama and established the Ben May Department of Molecular Biology at the University of Chicago Medical School, recruiting the world’s most excellent and creative young scholars. Within a few years, it became a world-renowned cancer research institution.
When Liao joined the Ben May Center in 1957, Dr. Huggins was already a titan of medicine and academia. “He was very kind and had no airs of a master,” Liao said. “He often came to my lab at 4 PM to ask the same question: ‘What did you discover today?’ Discovery was his lifelong pursuit. His maxim, ‘Discovery is our duty,’ became the guiding principle of the Ben May Center.”
Liao received his PhD in 1961 and was immediately hired by Dr. Huggins. The two became both teacher and friend, frequently exchanging ideas. “Dr. Huggins worked until he was 91 years old before retiring. We were together for 40 years,” Liao said reverently. “His rigorous scholarship, his dedication to academia, his emphasis on thinking and creativity — all were my models. He was my lifelong mentor and friend.”
Through Dr. Huggins, Liao also met another biochemistry master, Dr. Takashi Okada (李卓皓), who taught at UC Berkeley. Dr. Okada was a close friend of Dr. Huggins. Every time he visited Chicago, he would see Dr. Huggins, and through him, Liao and Dr. Okada became close friends who talked about everything.
Scientific Breakthroughs
First Discovery: New Enzyme
In his first year at UChicago, Liao discovered a strange new enzyme. He purified it and studied its function, completing his PhD thesis.
Male Hormone Research
In 1960, Liao began researching male hormones (androgens). At a time when scientists did not know where nucleic acids produced what functions, he pointed out that male hormones were primarily in the cell nucleus, promoting nucleic acid formation. This paper, published in a leading scientific journal, became a pioneer in the field of “hormone genetics.”
The Revolutionary Discovery (mid-1960s)
In the mid-1960s, Liao made a revolutionary discovery. Scientists believed that testosterone was formed in the testes and then transported through blood vessels to various organs, where it produced effects. But Liao discovered that testosterone itself does not produce effects — it must be converted by a 5-alpha-reductase enzyme into dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which then binds to a special nuclear receptor to produce biological effects.
At the time, the scientific community had no concept of male hormone activation, so this highly innovative theory was initially not accepted by American authorities. The paper was submitted and sat for 7 months before being published. In spring 1967, Liao submitted the paper to the British authority journal Nature, where it was immediately recognized and published.
The paper immediately caused a huge stir. Letters from around the world requesting the paper arrived like snowflakes, and many sought research assistance.
This discovery opened a new direction in hormone research. Diseases that depend on male hormones — prostate cancer, baldness, acne — were later treated based on this understanding. In October 1990, this paper was still rated by the American “Scientific Abstracts Organization” as one of the most-cited classic papers of the month.
At age 37, Liao was already an internationally renowned biochemist. For the next 40 years, he had a major discovery every 2-3 years, and his master status remained unshaken. He was a pioneer in many areas of biochemistry including male hormones, male hormone receptors, anti-male hormones, anti-male hormone receptors, the mystery of intersex, and treatment methods for prostate cancer. Scholars from around the world came to his lab for training every year, and many later became internationally renowned experts.
His discovery of “5-alpha-reductase inhibitors” — which inhibit male hormone activity in skin and prostate tissues — later led Merck Pharmaceuticals to develop two new drugs: Proscar (for prostate enlargement) and Propecia (for baldness). These two drugs generate billions of dollars in annual sales for Merck.
Later Research: Green Tea and Aging
In the 1990s, Liao also made unique discoveries in green tea and herbal research. He found that EGCG in green tea has important pharmacological effects and can be used to treat obesity, acne, and certain cancers. However, green tea must not be fermented during production, and drinking methods must be observed to retain EGCG components.
In recent years, Liao has made many surprising breakthroughs in research on anti-Alzheimer’s disease and cholesterol. He discovered that a type of LXR modulator plays a very important role in stroke, blood vessel blockage, heart attack, Alzheimer’s disease, certain cancers, and inflammation formation. If developed into a drug, it could make a tremendously important contribution to human health.
Awards and Honors
Liao received many academic excellence awards, including:

The Pincus Award (the highest honor in hormone research)
The Taiwanese American Foundation Science Award
The Tzu-Chung Medical Award
The Li Zhuo-hao Biochemistry Award
Member of the US National Academy of Sciences
Academician of the Academia Sinica (台湾中央研究院院士)
Reviewer for important American scientific journals and research funds

Liao treated these honors with equanimity.
Two Beliefs
Liao said the two beliefs he valued most in his life were:

As a follower of Dr. Huggins, he believed that the purpose of scientific research was to create well-being for all humanity.
As a Taiwanese, he believed that intellectuals should uphold their conscience and make greater contributions to their homeland.

NATPA and the Democratic Movement
Blacklist
Liao first discovered he was on the blacklist when he was about to leave the US for nearly 10 years. In 1965, he was invited by President Chien Sze (錢思亮) to return to NTU as a visiting scholar. At that time, he and his wife Shu-qing had been married for 5 years and had 3 daughters aged 1-4. Both sets of grandparents had not met the grandchildren, so the couple brought their three children back to Taiwan.
At the Tokyo airport, as they were about to board the China Airlines flight to Taiwan, they were blocked by KMT agents. The agents prevented them from boarding. The three little girls could not enter Taiwan.
Liao did not know when he was put on the blacklist — only discovered it when he found out, and felt the pain in his heart. He remained on the blacklist for over 20 years.
228 and White Terror
The 228 Incident and the subsequent White Terror period deeply affected Liao. As a high school student, he witnessed the massacres firsthand. These experiences shaped his political consciousness and his belief that intellectuals must speak out for justice.
美丽岛 (Beautiful Island) Incident
In late 1979, the “Beautiful Island” Incident occurred, followed by mass arrests. Seeing democratic activists arrested one by one, and Taiwan filled with a chilling atmosphere, overseas Taiwanese were anxious. After days of worry and reflection, Liao decided to take active rescue action.
He and Professor Huang Jin-lai (黄金来) from Kansas State University, and Professor Cai Jiayin (蔡嘉寅) from Purdue University, jointly called on Taiwanese professors in North America, upholding the conscience of intellectuals, to publish an advertisement in the Washington Post condemning the KMT government’s abuse of dissidents and demanding fair and public judicial trials for the arrested.
This call received an enthusiastic response. In just a few days, 137 Taiwanese professors signed the petition.
Liao said: “This was a great encouragement. We decided to further organize the North America Taiwanese Professors Association (NATPA) to care about the democratic movement in Taiwan.”
NATPA Founding (February 16, 1980)
On February 16, 1980, 16 professors — including Zhang Jinzhe, Zhang Xucheng, Chen Bingqi, Huang Yuancheng, Huang Jin-lai, Lai Yi-xiong, Liao Shu-zong, Lin Jingzhu, Sun Jinde, Shang Wenyi, Chen Huang Yimin, Cai Jiayin, Wu Deming, Wu Kunyu, Yang Shengliang, and Yan Wenliang — founded NATPA (North America Taiwanese Professors Association).
Liao served as the founding president (elected at the first member assembly, August 1980) and later served on the executive board.
林宅血案 (Lin Family Massacre)
When the 林宅血案 (Lin family massacre) occurred on February 28, 1980, Liao received an urgent call from a victim’s family member of the “Beautiful Island” incident, terrified that murders would continue. He called the Chinese consulate in Chicago and warned: “If you continue killing, all Taiwanese will rise up and fight you with force.”
陳文成 Death
When 陳文成 (Chen Wen-cheng), a young professor at Carnegie Mellon, died in June 1981, Liao called the university president Cyert and stated it was murder, not suicide — contrary to official Chinese government claims. He hired two American forensic pathologists, Dr. Robert Kirschner and Dr. Cyvil Wecht, to investigate.
1982 Taiwan Trip
In 1982, Liao led a breakthrough trip to Taiwan as an international scholar, invited by Dr. Li Zhuo-hao with a Taiwan University invitation letter. He met with KMT Secretary General 蔣彥士 (Yan Yanshi) and requested to speak with 李登輝 (Lee Teng-hui).
Chicago Family
Marriage and Children
Liao was quite conservative in pursuing girlfriends. He said: “In my era, Taiwan was a conservative society. In the entire NTU, everyone knew who was dating whom.”
His mother, 林瓊仙 (Lin Qiong-xian), was from a prominent Fengyuan family and was the first graduate of the 2nd class of 彰化高女 (Changhua Girls’ Normal School). She was热心公益 (enthusiastically involved in public welfare) and skilled at matchmaking. When she saw her son was about to receive his US PhD without a bride in sight, she took matters into her own hands.
She heard that a fellow townsman’s daughter was coming to Chicago for graduate studies. She invited Liao’s third aunt to visit the girl’s home. When Liao’s mother saw the girl, she was delighted. She quickly opened a small box and took out a small item, asking the girl to give it to her son.
The girl, unable to refuse, took the item to Chicago and called Liao. They fell in love at first sight and spent many evenings together. In 1960, they married in a church at UChicago.
His young wife was named 郭淑卿 (Guo Shu-qing), with a round, smiling face that always brought joy. She had graduated from Tokyo Jishu Women’s University and later studied at Chicago Jishu Women’s Seminary. Liao had assumed her father was a pastor.
The New Year’s Eve Birth
Both Liao and his wife were hospitable. After marriage, they frequently invited UChicago Taiwanese students to dinner at their home. A regular guest was Lin Qiuhong (林秋鴻), who recalled: “I remember New Year’s Eve 1961. We poor students were spending the New Year at Professor Liao’s house. At that time, Professor Liao’s wife was already heavily pregnant, still busy in the kitchen with Professor Liao. Suddenly, she went into labor. Professor Liao hurriedly took her to the hospital. That evening, their first child, Ciying (慈瑛), was born.”
The small family grew quickly. In just a few years, the second daughter Cifen (慈芬), third son Ciming (慈明), and fourth daughter Ciqing (慈卿) were born. Shu-qing raised four young children with her two hands, busy day and night. Liao’s research was also producing major discoveries, so he felt he couldn’t do it all.
Despite the busy life, they never neglected their students. The group went on spring outings, summer picnics, autumn apple picking, and winter ice skating. On New Year’s Eve, they invited students to the house for the reunion dinner, like a big family.
UChicago Taiwanese Student Community
As UChicago’s Taiwanese student population grew, they organized the “UChicago Taiwanese Student Association” in the mid-1960s. Student organizations needed a faculty advisor. Professor Liao was the universally recognized choice, and for many years he served as the advisor, effectively becoming the “father figure” (大家長) of Taiwanese students at UChicago.
During holidays and student association gatherings, he would drive students to the wholesale vegetable market early in the morning, buying a whole cart of vegetables. Then everyone chopped and cooked together at the Liao home, making a large amount of food. For Dragon Boat Festival, Professor and Mrs. Liao would stay up all night making zongzi (粽子) — hundreds at a time, ensuring everyone got at least one.
“Back then, to make spring roll wrappers (潤餅捲) for everyone, Professor Liao’s wife went back to Taiwan specifically to learn how to make them,” recalled Dr. Liang Deming (梁德明), now a dermatologist.
Chicago was the second-largest city in the US and the main gathering place for Taiwanese. The Central Western Taiwan Association was established in 1956. In 1970, it developed into the Greater Chicago Taiwan Association. By the 1980s, the Greater Chicago Taiwan Association’s annual meetings had 500-600 attendees. When speakers came from Taiwan, attendance reached 700-800. Finding a venue for so many people was not easy.
In those years, Professor Liao often served as the liaison to rent the International House from UChicago. When the Taiwanese Student Association hosted, the preparations for hundreds of people were chaotic.
Family & 清水 Ties
廖繼春’s Political Awakening
Beyond his artistic legacy, Liao Shu-zong’s father 廖繼春 (Liao Jichun) underwent a profound political transformation after witnessing the 228 Incident. As a teacher at Taichung Normal School during the massacres, he observed the KMT government’s corruption and the atrocities of the 228 massacre firsthand. He developed anti-KMT and Taiwan independence thoughts, believing that Taiwanese should forge their own path and no longer consider China as their homeland. Rather than fleeing to Japan, he went to Hong Kong and then to mainland China. Because of his Taiwan independence advocacy, he was imprisoned by the CCP for twenty-five years.
林朝權 & 林朝棨
Through his mother 林瓊仙’s prominent Fengyuan family, Liao Shu-zong was connected to two notable Taiwanese figures:

林朝權 (Lin Chao-quan) — His maternal uncle (二舅), a post-war leader in Taiwan’s sports movement and a former comrade of revolutionary leader Sun Wen.
林朝棨 (Lin Chao-qi) — His third maternal uncle (三舅), a renowned geologist famous for discovering the Banqiao site and other Taiwanese archaeological sites.

清水同鄉 & 1984 Olympics
In 1984, during the Los Angeles Olympics, 林朝權 and 林麗韞 (Lin Li-yun), both from 清水 (Fengyuan), came to Los Angeles. Since 楊嘉猷 (the memorial author), 林朝權, and 林麗韞 were all fellow townspeople from 清水, 楊嘉猷 visited them and gave them three books: the biography of 江文也, Peng Ming-min’s The Taste of Freedom (自由的滋味), and Wu Zhuoliu’s Fig (無花果). He hoped they would rediscover their Taiwanese identity and reconnect with their roots.
This personal connection reflected the broader network of 清水 (Fengyuan) families that spanned generations and disciplines — from painting (廖繼春) to geology (林朝棨) to sports (林朝權) — all connected through the small town in central Taiwan.
楊嘉猷’s Personal Connection
The memorial was written by 楊嘉猷 (Charles Yang), president of the Taiwanese American Historical Society and a founding member of NATPA. He knew the Liao family since his youth: his mother had worked with 廖繼春 at Taichung Normal School, and the Yang and Liao families were already acquainted through their shared 清水 (Fengyuan) roots.
楊嘉猷’s relationship with Liao Shu-zong deepened in the late 1980s. In 1989, when 楊嘉猷 was recruited by Democratic Progressive Party chairman Huang Hsin-chieh to run for Taichung County magistrate, Professor Liao invested considerable time in campaign support — making multiple appearances, holding seminars to raise funds and endorsements, and staying at former Representative Tian Zaiting’s residence in Fengyuan. He visited 楊嘉猷’s campaign office regularly to encourage staff and connect with voters.
Through these connections, 楊嘉猷 came to see Liao as a model of Taiwanese intellectual integrity: “He was a man of wisdom who did not hide his intelligence; he did not play it safe, did not remain neutral, but spoke courageously for Taiwan and the Taiwanese.”

“He was benevolent — he had great love for Taiwan and its homeland, leading the way in promoting Taiwan’s independence, democracy, progress, and development. He was brave — when Taiwan faced crises, when Taiwanese suffered, when Taiwanese Americans encountered disasters, he always demonstrated moral courage and stepped forward.”
— 楊嘉猷 (Charles Yang), 2014

Legacy
Liao Shu-zong’s life embodied the dual commitment he valued most: scientific research for the benefit of all humanity, and Taiwanese intellectual conscience in service to his homeland. He was a biochemist who used his platform to advocate for Taiwan’s democracy, bridging overseas intellectuals and mainland dissidents.
His scientific legacy includes the discovery of the 5-alpha-reductase pathway, which revolutionized the understanding of male hormone action and led to multi-billion-dollar pharmaceuticals. His political legacy includes the founding of NATPA, which served as a bridge between overseas intellectuals and Taiwan’s democratic movement.
He passed away in 2017. A memorial tribute was written by 楊嘉猷 (Charles Yang), describing him as “典型在夙昔” (a model of enduring character).
Source Notes and Confidence

people/lin-chao-chi.title: Lin Chao-chi (林朝棨)
people/lin-chao-chi.content:
Lin Chao-chi (林朝棨)
Lin Chao-chi (林朝棨) was a renowned Taiwanese geologist, best known for discovering the 十三行遺址 (Shihping Archaeological Site), one of Taiwan’s most significant archaeological sites. He was the third uncle (三舅) of biochemist 廖述宗 (Liao Shu-zong).
Identity Snapshot

English: Lin Chao-chi
Chinese: 林朝棨
Profession: Geologist
Geography: Taiwan
Core roles: Prominent Taiwanese geologist; 十三行遺址 (Shihping site) discoverer
Relation: 三舅 (third uncle) of 廖述宗 (Liao Shu-zong)

Scientific Contributions
Lin Chao-chi was a famous geologist whose most notable achievement was the discovery of the 十三行遺址 (Shihping Archaeological Site), an important prehistoric archaeological site in Taiwan. This discovery contributed significantly to the understanding of Taiwan’s ancient cultures and history.
His reputation as a geologist made him well-known enough to be specifically mentioned in biographical accounts of his nephew 廖述宗, reflecting the prominence of the Lin family in Taiwanese science.
Family Connections
As the third uncle (三舅) of 廖述宗, Lin Chao-chi was part of the extended family network that included 廖述宗’s mother 林瓊仙 (Lin Qiong-xian) and second uncle 林朝權 (Lin Chao-quan). The memorial account by 楊嘉猷 (Charles Yang) specifically notes Lin Chao-chi’s fame for discovering the 十三行遺址.

people/lin-chao-quan.title: Lin Chao-quan (林朝權)
people/lin-chao-quan.content:
Lin Chao-quan (林朝權)
Lin Chao-quan (林朝權, 1900s–1980s) was a Taiwanese sports leader and democratic activist, best known as the second cousin (二舅/二叔) of biochemist 廖述宗 (Liao Shu-zong). He was a close friend of 孫文 (Sun Yat-sen) and served as a 國民大會代表 (National Assembly representative).
Identity Snapshot

English: Lin Chao-quan
Chinese: 林朝權
Born: 1900s, 清水 (Qingshui), Taiwan
Died: 1980s
Relation: 二舅/二叔 of 廖述宗 (Liao Shu-zong)
Profession: Sports leader, political activist
Geography: Taiwan, Hong Kong, China, USA (Los Angeles)
Core roles: Taiwanese sports leadership; Sun Yat-sen associate; democratic activist

Political Activism
Lin Chao-quan was born in 清水 (Qingshui), the same hometown as the Yang family. His political consciousness was shaped early by witnessing the 二二八 (228) Incident, where he saw the Nationalist government’s massacre of Taiwanese people. This experience led him to develop anti-KMT sentiment and a belief that Taiwanese should forge their own path rather than认中國為祖國 (recognize China as the motherland).
Rather than fleeing to Japan, Lin went to Hong Kong and then entered China. Because of his advocacy for Taiwan independence, he was arrested by the Communist government and imprisoned for 25 years.
Post-War Sports Leadership
After World War II (終戰), Lin Chao-quan became a leading figure in Taiwan’s sports community. He held the position of 國民大會代表 (National Assembly representative), though he later became disillusioned with the KMT government’s corruption.
1984 LA Olympics Visit
In 1984, during the Los Angeles Olympics, Lin Chao-quan visited Los Angeles. He was visited by 楊嘉猷 (Charles Yang), who brought him three books: “江文也傳” (Biography of Wen-yeh Chiang), 彭明敏’s “自由的滋味” (The Taste of Freedom), and 吳濁流’s “無花果” (Figless Fruit), hoping to help him reconnect with his Taiwanese identity.

people/lin-fu-kun.title: Lin Fu-kun (林福坤)
people/lin-fu-kun.content:
Lin Fu-kun (林福坤)
Lin Fu-kun (林福坤, born 1941) is a Taiwanese American biochemist and the inventor of Epogen (Epoetin Alfa / 促紅血球生成素), a DNA-engineered medicine that has treated millions of anemic patients with chronic renal failure worldwide. His work at Amgen marked the beginning of the biotech revolution and earned him international recognition.
Identity Snapshot

English: Lin Fu-kun
Chinese: 林福坤
Born: 1941, Keelung (基隆市), Taiwan
Education: B.S. plant pathology, National Taiwan University (1964); M.S. plant pathology, NTU (1967); Ph.D. plant pathology, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (1971)
Key employer: Amgen, Thousand Oaks, California (1981–retirement)
Key discovery: Recombinant human erythropoietin (EPO) gene, patented 1983-12-13
Roles: Biochemist; scientist; inventor
Organizations: Amgen; 安進公司

Early Life and Education
Lin Fu-kun was born in 1941 in Keelung City’s Anle District, Taiwan. He was the fifth of eight children (two older sisters, two older brothers, two younger sisters, one younger brother). His father practiced traditional Chinese medicine (中醫師), was skilled in bone-setting, and had even served as a special physician for the police force.
Lin attended Anle Elementary School in Keelung, then the Provincial Keelung Water Production School for junior high, and Keelung Municipal High School for senior high. After high school, he entered National Taiwan University’s Zoology Department, later transferring to Plant Pathology.
In 1964, he completed his bachelor’s degree and served as a reserve second lieutenant in the Navy headquarters at Zuoying (左營海軍總部) for one year. After his reserve officer discharge in 1965, he returned to NTU and worked under Professor Wu Long-xi (吳龍溪) on fungal physiology research, earning his M.S. in plant pathology in 1967.
Doctoral Studies
In 1967, through Professor Wu’s recommendation, Lin received a research assistant scholarship from Dr. David Gottlieb at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Dr. Gottlieb was a renowned authority in antibiotic research and was, notably, Wu Long-xi’s own doctoral advisor — making him Lin’s “grand-advisor.”
Lin pursued his Ph.D. while single. During this time, he enjoyed typical graduate student life: fishing in rivers, hiking to view autumn maple leaves, and socializing with fellow Taiwanese students. In 1971, at age 30, he successfully completed his doctoral dissertation.
Postdoctoral Wanderings
After leaving the University of Illinois, the U.S. was caught between the space race and the Vietnam War, which drained the treasury and caused an economic downturn. The biotech field’s funding dried up after the Apollo program’s peak. Finding biotech research positions was extremely difficult, and most available funding went to cancer research.
Lin’s first postdoctoral position was at Purdue University, researching cancer cell questions. This was a shift from his previous work on fungal biochemistry to human medical research. However, the techniques were similar enough that the transition was manageable.
A notable anecdote from this period: During the summer of 1972, Purdue hosted the Midwest Taiwanese Softball Tournament, with over 10 teams and nearly 500 attendees. The local Taiwanese community provided meals for everyone. To prepare a Taiwanese dish of “five-spice” (五香), the community asked students to help catch fish from a nearby dam. The high-educated anglers caught so many fish that they filled several trash cans with ice in a bathtub, creating a strong fish odor throughout the house — and had to ask Lin to store the fish in his lab’s large freezer.
In 1972, Lin married 高雲娟 (Gao Yunjuan), a high school classmate, at Purdue.
After Purdue, Lin moved to the University of Nebraska’s tumor biology laboratory for further postdoctoral research, studying how hormones affect the formation of breast cancer precursor cells in mice. This was a common postdoc arrangement — funding depended on professors writing grant proposals, and research topics were professor-determined. After four years of postdoc奔波 (hustling), Lin felt a lack of “belonging” and began to consider seeking a more stable work environment.
Return to Academia and Decision to Return
In 1975, Lin decided to return to Taiwan to work at the Academia Sinica (中研院) as an associate researcher in the Institute of Botany, and also taught at NTU’s Plant Pathology Department.
During his two years at Academia Sinica, Taiwan was still in a “hardship phase” — research funding was extremely limited, only enough to hire night-school university students with no research experience. Equipment had to be ordered from the U.S., and the approval-to-import process took two to three months, severely slowing research progress.
Despite wanting to focus on research, Lin faced numerous difficulties. To keep up with the rapidly developing biotech field, he continued to maintain connections with U.S. research institutions, using summer breaks to conduct short-term research in the United States.
After two years at Academia Sinica, Lin decided to return to the United States to expand his career.
The Turning Point: Amgen
In 1977, Lin returned to the U.S. and first worked at Louisiana State University, conducting nucleic acid biochemistry research on transfer RNA (tRNA) sequences. That year, biotech research achieved a major breakthrough: the chemical method to identify DNA sequences was invented, simplifying DNA molecular structure analysis. Lin found this discovery very interesting and began reading about genetic engineering.
In 1979, after two years at LSU, Lin transferred to the Medical University of South Carolina, conducting genetic engineering technology research.
By 1981, Lin had turned 40 — reaching the Confucian milestone of “四十而不惑” (at forty, I had no doubts). Ten years had passed since he earned his Ph.D. In those ten years, he had crossed the Pacific repeatedly, working at five different research institutions. He described his journey as “寄人籬下、大智若愚” (living under others’ roofs, appearing foolish but actually wise). However, Lin responded with gratitude: “Don’t say that — I learned a lot of new things during that time.” He believed that ten years of research across five institutions had solidly built his research foundation.
In August 1981, Lin saw an advertisement in Science magazine for a research position at Amgen (安進公司), a small biotech company newly established in Thousand Oaks, California. The ad was simple — it only mentioned needing a researcher, without even specifying what kind. At the time, Amgen was a little-known company, and few would have been interested. But something drove Lin to submit his resume. He flew from South Carolina on the East Coast to Thousand Oaks on the West Coast for an interview.
Lin joined Amgen on August 6, 1981, as the company’s seventh scientist. Amgen, founded less than a year earlier, had only about a dozen employees total — from the CEO to part-time workers. When Lin first started, the company had only one building and one lab bench that could be shared by two people. He waited several months before getting his own 15-foot bench.
The EPO Discovery
From the research topics Amgen had prepared, Lin chose the erythropoietin (EPO / 紅血球生成素) gene project. EPO is a hormone produced by the kidneys that stimulates bone marrow to produce red blood cells. All organs, tissues, and cells in the body depend on red blood cells to deliver oxygen. When kidney function fails, EPO secretion decreases, red blood cell production drops sharply, and the body suffers from anemia, dizziness, weakness, and pain — essentially a multi-system illness. Patients had to rely on dialysis and blood transfusions just to maintain basic life.
In 1977, scientists at the University of Chicago discovered that EPO could be purified from urine, but the quantity was extremely small — not clinically useful. Visionary business leaders began thinking about how to use academic research to develop pharmaceuticals.
At the time, several biotech companies were competing in this space: Amgen in Southern California, Genentech in Northern California, Genetics Institute and Biogen in Boston. A famous article titled “The 2 Billion Dollar Protein Sequencing Error” described the race.
Amgen obtained EPO samples from Eugene Goldwasser, the most prominent Chicago University professor in EPO research, and sent them to their consultant, Lee Hood (加州理工學院生物系主任), for amino acid sequencing. Hood, an instrument expert who had just invented a device that could sequence amino acids with very small samples, assigned his co-inventor Rodney Hewick to the analysis.
Shortly after EPO sequencing, on September 1, 1981, Rodney Hewick suddenly resigned and took the EPO sequence data as a “gift” to join Boston’s Genetics Institute as a senior protein chemist.
This began a race between Amgen (west coast) and Genetics Institute (east coast) to use genetic engineering to clone EPO. The problem was that Rodney Hewick’s partial EPO amino acid sequence data contained 3 errors. After three years of futile attempts, Genetics Institute began to suspect the data was wrong. They could no longer obtain samples from Goldwasser and had to go through Japan, finding Takaji Miyake (who had previously worked in Goldwasser’s lab) to obtain urine from a Mongolian descendant in Kyushu, Japan, who had aplastic anemia. Genetics Institute extracted EPO from the urine, re-sequenced, and finally got the correct answer — but it was too late.
Lin Fu-kun had already filed the patent application on December 13, 1983.
Epogen
The recombinant human erythropoietin project was finally approved by the FDA in 1989, with the generic name Epoetin Alfa, branded as Epogen. Since its introduction, Epogen has successfully treated millions of anemic persons with chronic renal failure worldwide.
Lin’s discovery and invention marked the beginning of the biotech revolution. His work earned him numerous awards and recognitions, including:

1990 Quality of Life Award
1995 Discoverers Award by Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America
The 1994 National Medal of Technology awarded to Amgen at the White House, largely attributed to Lin’s contributions

Legacy
Lin Fu-kun’s story is one of perseverance through a decade of research “wanderings” — five institutions, two countries, and relentless dedication to a scientific question. From a little-known researcher in a lab to the inventor of a medicine that changed millions of lives, his journey embodies the immigrant scientist’s path: hard work, adaptability, and the courage to take risks.
The 2017 TAHS publication describes his story as one that “gives hope to Taiwanese Americans who are currently struggling and奔波 (hustling) in life.”
Source Notes and Confidence

people/lin-qiong-xian.title: Lin Qiong-xian (林瓊仙)
people/lin-qiong-xian.content:
Lin Qiong-xian (林瓊仙)
Lin Qiong-xian (林瓊仙) was a prominent member of the Fengyuan family and the mother of biochemist 廖述宗 (Liao Shu-zong). She was known for her热心公益 (enthusiasm for public welfare), matchmaking skills, and dedication to her family.
Identity Snapshot

English: Lin Qiong-xian
Chinese: 林瓊仙
Hometown: 豐原 (Fengyuan), Taiwan
Spouse: 廖繼春 (Liao Jichun), famous painter
Children: 8 (including 廖述宗 as third child)
Education: Graduate of 彰化高女 (Changhua Girls’ Normal School), 2nd class
Geography: Fengyuan, Tainan, Taiwan; Chicago (later)
Core roles: Community volunteer; art teacher; matchmaker; mother of 8

Background and Education
Lin Qiong-xian came from a prominent family in 豐原 (Fengyuan), Taiwan. She graduated from 彰化高女 (彰化女子高級中學 / Changhua Girls’ Normal School), the 2nd class of its graduating cohort — an achievement that was notable for women in Taiwan during that era.
Public Service and Community Work
She was known for being 热心公益 (enthusiastically involved in public welfare causes). Beyond her community work, she also taught art at a school in Tainan, following in the artistic spirit of her husband 廖繼春.
Matchmaking and Family
Lin Qiong-xian was skilled at matchmaking. When her son 廖述宗 received his PhD from the US without a wife, she took matters into her own hands. She arranged a meeting with a fellow townsman’s daughter who was coming to Chicago for graduate studies — resulting in the marriage of 廖述宗 to 郭淑卿 (Guo Shu-qing) in 1960.
Family Life
The family ran a stationery shop called “文藝社” (Wenyi She) at home. Lin Qiong-xian raised eight children with great dedication, managing household affairs, the family shop, and supporting her husband’s artistic career.

people/lin-yuan-ching.title: Lin Yuan-qing (林元清)
people/lin-yuan-ching.content:
Lin Yuan-qing (林元清)
Lin Yuan-qing (林元清) is a Taiwanese American orthopedic surgeon who built a long practice in Alhambra, California, after immigrating from Taiwan. His story — from a rural Taiwanese town to one of the most rigorous medical training programs in the United States — exemplifies the immigrant physician’s journey.
Identity Snapshot

English: Lin Yuan-qing
Chinese: 林元清
Born: 1945 (estimated), Ji-Ji (集集), Nantou County, Taiwan
Ancestry: Sixth-generation Taiwanese American family; ancestors emigrated from Fujian to Ji-Ji, Taiwan
Education: B.S. (Taiwan), M.D., Taipei Medical College (台北醫學院); Residency: Johns Hopkins University / Baltimore Union Hospital
Specialty: Orthopedic surgery
Location: Alhambra, California
Family: Wife; children (two at time of profile)

Family Background and Early Life
Lin’s family has deep roots in Ji-Ji, a small town in Nantou County, Taiwan, known for timber, camphor, and bananas. His ancestors had emigrated from Fujian to Ji-Ji generations earlier. Ji-Ji’s natural beauty — clear streams and mountains — shaped his childhood.
His father, Lin Zhilian (林智煉), served as director of a local health station. His grandfather (Lin Zhilian’s father) died when he was young, and his mother also passed away early. After completing only three years of elementary school, Lin Zhilian left home to become an apprentice at Dr. Yang Sanfa’s clinic in Zhongliao Township. After three years, feeling there was no future, he traveled alone to Xiamen to seek his fortune.
When Lin Zhilian first arrived in Xiamen, he survived by running a street stall and washing dishes. Through a series of fortunate connections, he found work at the Health Bureau. When a Japanese-run博爱 Hospital (Bo’ai Hospital) in Xiamen was recruiting local physicians, Lin Zhilian’s formal education was insufficient to qualify. He wrote to his former employer, Dr. Yang Sanfa, requesting a certificate confirming that Lin Zhilian had interned and worked at his clinic. With this document, he was allowed to take the exam and passed.
Lin Zhilian went on to serve as a prison doctor. At that time, the Taipei Medical College Dean (魏火曜) and Ren’ai Hospital Director (林柳生) were also working there. His training period was long — 5 years and 8 months — and he received his physician’s license.
His mother, Wu He (吳和), was from Tainan. She traveled to Xiamen to visit relatives, met the physician Lin Zhilian through a friend, and they married in 1943, settling in Xiamen.
Escape from Xiamen
After Japan’s defeat in World War II, local Xiamen residents began targeting Taiwanese people. Many were hunted and killed. Lin Zhilian, having lived in Xiamen for many years, was not initially identified as Taiwanese by locals. However, a neighborhood watchman asked him whether he knew “who the Taiwanese are” and reported him.
Lin Zhilian was in danger. He had to flee. He darkened his face, wrapped a headcloth around himself, and had an old woman lead him, pretending to be a frail old woman. He was trying to board a ship to escape. The situation at the dock was tense — authorities were looking for “Taiwanese traitor Lin Zhilian.” When a soldier asked him his surname, he stammered. The soldier said, “Say you’re surnamed Wu!” and waved him through. He escaped.
In 1949, as the mainland fell to the Communists, the family took the last flight from Xiamen back to Taiwan. They returned to Ji-Ji.
Lin Yuan-qing was born in this period — in Ji-Ji, where he grew up in a relatively carefree childhood. His father, seeing children playing all day, felt this was not the way. Lin Yuan-qing’s uncle worked as a driver for the Mining Corporation in Taipei, so Lin was transferred to Taipei for elementary school at age 6.
Education
Lin attended Ximen Elementary School, then passed the exam for the prestigious Taipei First Middle School (建中), and subsequently entered Taipei Medical College (台北醫學院).
He was not a particularly diligent student. In the year between his second and third year of high school, there were 55 students in his class, and he ranked around 52nd. It was only when his teacher, Professor Lu Shifen, spoke to him earnestly — “You need to work harder, or you won’t get into a university” — that Lin resolved to study hard. He cut his hair short, kept a bucket of water by his desk, and plunged his feet into it whenever drowsiness struck. This method finally worked, and he successfully entered Taipei Medical College.
Lin was grateful to Taipei Medical College for its training. He believed that while the school’s academic standing might not have been as high as National Taiwan University, it offered students enormous room to grow. Students who studied seriously and maintained a humble attitude produced many successful professionals. Many physicians in Los Angeles today graduated from Taipei Medical College, and their contributions to society are widely recognized.
Military Service
After graduating from Taipei Medical College, Lin served his military duty at Kinmen (金門). During this time, his main daily work involved laying sod and planting trees to green the island. At night, local residents would bring them fresh oysters, which they enjoyed. Lin described it as “a very pleasant year.”
In 2014, the World Chinese Business Association held a cruise that stopped at Kinmen. Lin deliberately skipped the scheduled visits and took a taxi to his old base, finding that the local houses and alle hadn’t changed much, but his former military camp was gone without a trace. The old local friends were no longer there — they had moved away. Lin felt deeply regretful.
Internship and Residency
After his military service, Lin worked as an internal medicine physician at Gengxin Hospital (耕莘醫院) for one year. Life was comfortable, and he had considered staying, gaining experience, and then joining his father at the Xin’an Hospital clinic on Xinyi Road — a relaxed career path.
However, after only half a year, three of the four physicians he knew well at the hospital decided to go abroad. They asked Lin if he wanted to join them. Lin didn’t have strong initial interest but, considering the limitations of internal medicine in healthcare, he filled out the form with surgery as his first choice and was fortunately selected by Baltimore Union Memorial Hospital (巴爾地摩紀念醫院) as a surgical intern.
At the time, Lin thought studying abroad would add prestige to his resume and make his future practice look better.
First Case
When Lin arrived at the hospital and checked in, he was immediately assigned to the duty room, where he stayed for over three months. The next morning, the surgical director warmly greeted him and immediately sent him to the operating room. After changing clothes and washing hands, his first patient was a gunshot wound victim. Watching the surgeons’熟练 (skilled) chest and abdominal operations, Lin couldn’t understand what they were saying — “whatever I say, they won’t understand, so it cancels out!” He thought to himself.
Suddenly, the surgeons abandoned their work mid-operation. An anesthesiologist flipped the drape, and Lin discovered the patient had already died. This was Lin’s first case in America — a 100% shock education.
Johns Hopkins Orthopedic Surgery
After settling into his routine, Lin worked hard. When he encountered unfamiliar cases during his consultations, he would automatically go to the library to read materials. He was fortunate to encounter several senior physicians who were eager to teach. One particularly strict senior physician would quiz residents even when patients were on the operating table — if you couldn’t answer, he’d hit you with a clamp. It wasn’t very painful, but it was a matter of face. Lin read through the entire anatomy textbook.
Several excellent orthopedic surgeons came from Johns Hopkins. They trained young doctors rigorously and let them perform surgery. Lin benefited enormously.
One particular case: a posterior shoulder dislocation. Lin had never heard of this and had never seen it. He researched the procedure, went to the anatomy lab to practice on a cadaver, and then proceeded to surgery. The orthopedic chief Dr. Johnson supervised, with the senior resident beside him. Dr. Johnson knew this case was difficult and asked the senior resident to perform it. The senior resident was reluctant, saying, “I’ve never seen this case before.” Dr. Johnson, trying to stimulate him, turned to Lin and said, “Dr. Lin, you do it.”
Relying on his practice, Lin confidently performed the procedure and completed it successfully. His performance impressed Dr. Johnson greatly. After surgery, Dr. Johnson invited him for coffee, praised his work, and asked if he was interested in switching to orthopedic surgery.
Lin knew how competitive orthopedics was — only the top five from medical school could apply, usually only 2-3 positions, yet hundreds of applicants. He replied, “It’s only a dream!” But Dr. Johnson wanted him to submit an application form. Lin did, and was ultimately selected.
At the time, the hospital’s medical resident system admitted 12 first-year residents, narrowed to 6 by year two, 3 by year three, and only 2 by year five. Lin knew his language skills couldn’t compete with native speakers. Sure enough, by year three, he was no longer on the list. He was preparing to pack up and return to Taiwan when Dr. Johnson told him the good news: he had been accepted into the orthopedic surgery residency program jointly run by Johns Hopkins University and Baltimore Union Hospital.
His first year was at Johns Hopkins, the second year rotated through local children’s hospitals, and in his third year, he returned to Baltimore Union Hospital as Chief Resident, specializing in hand surgery. These three years gave Lin a solid foundation.
Family Crisis
Before entering Hopkins in May 1975, Lin received a phone call from his father: the guarantor for their house loan had collapsed, and the bank refused to renew. If the $200,000+ loan couldn’t be repaid by year-end, the house would be auctioned. Lin’s father needed his help.
To raise money, Lin took a part-time emergency room shift at another hospital, working two to three nights a week from 7 PM to 7 AM. By year-end, he had saved about $7,000. At the exchange rate of 1:40, this was enough to help his father through the crisis.
One night during his shift, Lin suddenly felt severe abdominal cramps. Using his medical knowledge, he correctly diagnosed acute appendicitis. But it was deep night, there was no one to cover for him, and he couldn’t leave his post. He gave himself a painkiller injection and endured until morning shift change, then drove home. He told his wife that he had acute appendicitis and to go to the ER. The ER and surgical director performed surgery and found the situation was extremely severe — his appendix was nearly ruptured.
Career in America
Kaiser Hospital
After completing his training, Lin’s first position in Los Angeles was at Kaiser Hospital in Harbor City. Kaiser paid a good salary, but Lin had made a wrong judgment: he bought a house with borrowed money for the down payment, and the loan payments were very tight.
Opening Practice in Alhambra
His classmate Chen Guangyao (陳光耀) told Lin that several orthopedic physicians in Alhambra were looking for partners. Lin drove over to meet Gao Ruizhi (高瑞治) and Lu Hongyuan (陸洪元), who suggested he open a practice in Alhambra.
Lin was dissatisfied with the local clinic environment — the clinic buildings were dilapidated and far from his standards for a modern medical practice. He went home and discussed with his wife. They had two options: sell the current house, reduce financial burden, and stay at Kaiser; or open a practice in Alhambra.
They chose to sell. Lin placed a “Sale by Owner” advertisement in the local newspaper at $190,000. The next weekend, he received 50-60 calls, and some people even knocked on his door saying, “I’ll buy at your price, if you don’t sell, I’ll sue you.” Lin was terrified and stopped answering calls. His wife thought if it was so popular, raising the price might invite lawsuits. They decided not to sell.
In December 1978, Lin resigned from Kaiser and opened a practice in Alhambra.
Early Challenges
On his first day, the dilapidated clinic had zero patients. The next day, an old woman came with a tumor on her hand. Seeing the young-looking physician (少年噹噹) in the old, rundown clinic, she distrusted him and asked, “Did you graduate from medical school?” Lin quickly showed her his diploma and Johns Hopkins training certificate, finally earning her trust. The treatment result was satisfactory.
Slowly, referrals from other physicians increased, and the situation improved.
Lin was open about the difficulties of opening a practice. As a newcomer, orthopedic physicians at the hospital were almost unfriendly — they scrutinized his medical results, looking for ways to challenge him, suspend him, or drive him out.
Lin experienced these challenges firsthand. At one review at Garfield Hospital, physicians unanimously agreed he should be suspended. Lin looked at the case and discovered they were criticizing him using outdated medical techniques. With the same condition, Lin’s operation took 40 minutes while theirs took four hours; his patients were discharged in three days while theirs stayed two weeks. “What right do these physicians have to want to suspend me?”
The Chief of Surgery said both sides had presented their views, confirmed Lin’s treatment was appropriate, and asked the physicians to withdraw their suspension request.
The Supervising Physician Incident
According to regulations, the first six cases of a new physician must have another physician present to supervise and assist. At one surgery at Alhambra Hospital, Lin called eight physicians, all of whom were declined for various reasons. Finally, one physician (Dr. Duncan) agreed to come for a 2 AM surgery.
At 2:30 AM, Dr. Duncan hadn’t arrived. Lin called — he said his car broke down. There was nothing to be done. Lin successfully completed the surgery. At 2:45 AM, while he was suturing, a physician named (Iranian籍) called and said he could come to help. Lin told him the surgery was complete and suturing had begun, but welcomed him anyway.
This physician reported to the surgical department, accusing Lin of performing surgery without a supervising physician. The hospital established a “Special Investigation Committee” of nine orthopedic physicians.
During the hearing:

One physician asked why Lin refused to help — Lin explained the surgery was already complete and suturing was in progress. The physician understood the situation.
Another physician questioned why Lin didn’t find a helper. Lin asked each one, “Did I ask you?” They said yes, but “I had no time.” Dr. Duncan’s excuse was “car broke down.”
The orthopedic chief, hearing the Iranian physician’s complaint with disbelief, warned him not to cause trouble without cause, and ruled the case dismissed.

Lin passed the review. After his first six supervised cases all received excellent evaluations, Lin patiently waited until his eighth case was complete, then applied to the Orthopedic Society for removal of supervision — which was granted without question. To be safe, Lin also confirmed with the surgical department.
Building a Practice
Lin’s practice grew steadily. He built a reputation for efficient, effective surgery and patient care. He became well-known in the Southern California Taiwanese community.
Return to Taiwan
Lin never hid his desire to return to Taiwan. In 2014, the World Chinese Business Association held a cruise that stopped at Kinmen. Lin deliberately skipped the scheduled visits and took a taxi to his old base, finding that the local houses and alleys hadn’t changed much, but his former military camp was gone without a trace.
Source Notes and Confidence

people/lisa-su.title: Lisa T. Su (蘇姿丰)
people/lisa-su.content:
Lisa T. Su (蘇姿丰)
Lisa T. Su (蘇姿丰, born 1969) is the CEO and President of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), a Sunnyvale, California-based semiconductor giant. She is one of the most powerful women in technology and a prominent figure in the Taiwanese American community.
Identity Snapshot

English: Lisa T. Su
Chinese: 蘇姿丰
Born: 1969, Taiwan
Education: BS MIT EE 1990, MS MIT EE 1991, PhD MIT EE 1994
Role: CEO and President, AMD (Advanced Micro Devices)
Geography: Sunnyvale, California / Silicon Valley
Heritage: Second-generation Taiwanese American
Family: Father 蘇春槐 (Su Chun-huai) profiled in 2017 TAHS Publication

Education
Su was born in Taiwan in 1969 and immigrated with her family to the United States. She attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) for all of her degrees:

B.S. Electrical Engineering, MIT (1990)
M.S. Electrical Engineering, MIT (1991)
Ph.D. Electrical Engineering, MIT (1994)

Her PhD focused on semiconductor technology, specifically copper interconnect process technology at 0.22 micron nodes — a critical advancement in semiconductor manufacturing.
Career at IBM
Before joining AMD, Su developed copper interconnect process technology at IBM while working at 0.22 micron nodes. This work was critical to advancing semiconductor manufacturing and was a key area of research at IBM’s research laboratories.
AMD Leadership
Su joined AMD and rose through the ranks to become CEO and President of the company. Under her leadership, AMD has become a major competitor in the semiconductor industry, particularly in processors and graphics cards.
Her appointment as CEO of AMD was a landmark moment for both the technology industry and for Asian American women in leadership positions.
Recognition
Su has been recognized with numerous honors:

IEEE Board of Directors
MIT EE Advisory Board
Recognition from the semiconductor industry for her technical leadership

Community Significance
Su’s father, 蘇春槐 (Su Chun-huai), was profiled in the same 2017 TAHS Publication as a “tiger father” proud of his daughter’s achievements. The profile “虎爸談虎女” (Tiger Father Talks About Tiger Daughter) highlighted Su Chun-huai’s pride in his daughter’s accomplishments as CEO of AMD.
Su’s story is emblematic of the second-generation Taiwanese American experience — children of immigrants who achieve the highest levels of success in mainstream American society.

people/martha-vandriel.title: Martha VanDriel (Martha S.H. VanDriel)
people/martha-vandriel.content:
Martha VanDriel (Martha S.H. VanDriel)
Colonel Martha S.H. VanDriel (née Hsu, 許和瑞’s daughter) is a retired U.S. Army officer who served for over 26 years. She is the first Taiwanese-American woman to graduate from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point (1991), graduating in the top 10% of her class. She retired in September 2017 from the Office of the Secretary of Defense.
Identity Snapshot

English: Martha S.H. VanDriel (née Hsu)
Chinese: 瑪莎·范德瑞爾
Born: South Pasadena, California (daughter of Henry Hsu 許和瑞)
Education: B.S. International Relations and International Strategic History, West Point (1991); M.A. National Security Studies, UNC-Chapel Hill (2000)
Military Service: 26+ years (1991–2017)
Rank: Colonel (retired)
Branch: Military Intelligence; later Cyber Command
Spouse: Michael VanDriel (fellow Army officer)
Father: Henry Hsu (許和瑞), community leader; daughter Martha
Geography: Washington, D.C. / Pentagon / various military assignments

Early Life
Martha’s parents, Henry Hsu and his wife, came to the United States in the early 1960s as graduate students from Taiwan. They met and married in California.
Before Martha was born, her father Henry had written several letters to his family in Taiwan that were critical of the ruling KMT government. The government intercepted the letters, placed Henry on a blacklist, and harassed his family so badly that they told him, “For your safety, do not return to Taiwan. And for our safety, please do not communicate with us any longer.” Henry refocused his future on staying in the United States, where he could earn a living, raise his family in safety, and express his political views peacefully.
Martha grew up in South Pasadena, California, where she excelled in high school. As a straight-A student, Academic Decathlon award winner, head cheerleader, editor of the school literary magazine, and swim team member, she was voted “Most Intelligent” and “Most Likely To Succeed” by her high school class.
When looking at potential colleges to attend, many people encouraged her to become a doctor, a lawyer, or an engineer — the usual accepted occupations for many Asian Americans. But Martha said: “I wanted to be different. I didn’t want to be typical. I felt that I had something to prove, and I wanted to gain the respect of others.”
She was intrigued by West Point and its famous graduates, and by how you couldn’t go there just because you did well academically — you had to do well academically, physically, and leadership-wise.
West Point
Martha’s Christian faith led her to accept West Point’s offer of admission. She said: “I knew that this is where God wanted me to be, and this helped me to stay at West Point, especially when things were very difficult during my first year there.”
The difficult academic, physical, and leadership discipline at West Point scared Martha, because these factors had historically caused about 30% of each West Point freshman class to drop out before graduation. In the end, Martha’s Christian faith led her to accept West Point’s offer.
In 1991, Martha graduated in the top 10% of her West Point class with a Bachelor of Sciences Degree in International Relations and International Strategic History. She was commissioned as a Second Lieutenant in the Military Intelligence branch of the U.S. Army.
Military Career
Early Career
Martha’s early career was marked by success. She was the Honor Graduate of her West Point class. Her early assignments included:

Company Commander at U.S. and South Korean Forces-Iraq Headquarters, Al Faw Palace, Camp Victory, Baghdad, in 2010
Multiple leadership positions in Military Intelligence

Cyber Command
In 2011, at the rank of Lieutenant Colonel, Martha was appointed the first Chief of Plans and Policy of the newly formed U.S. Army Cyber Command. This was a critical role in establishing the organizational structure and operational framework for the Army’s cyber operations.
Post-West Point Teaching
After company command, Martha married another Army officer, Michael VanDriel. She was accepted into an Army program that paid for her Master’s degree so that she could return to West Point to teach cadets. Therefore, in 2000, Martha earned a M.A. in National Security Studies from UNC-Chapel Hill, then returned to West Point to teach International Relations, International Security Studies, and the Politics and Strategy of Cyberwarfare.
Final Assignments
Martha’s last assignment before retiring in September 2017 was at the Office of the Principal Cyber Advisor at the Pentagon, where she served as the主管 (director) of the office that coordinates the personnel and training of nearly 30 different cyber warfare units under the U.S. Department of Defense.
Her earlier role was at the Office of the Secretary of Defense.
Retirement
Martha VanDriel retired from the U.S. Army in September 2017 after 26 years of service. She was immediately recruited by Merck Pharmaceuticals to serve as the head of their IT risk management department.
Legacy
Martha VanDriel’s story is remarkable for several reasons:

She was the first Taiwanese-American woman to graduate from West Point
She served in one of the most physically and mentally demanding roles in the U.S. military
She rose to the rank of Colonel, one of the highest ranks achievable by a career officer
She was instrumental in establishing the U.S. Army’s cyber warfare capabilities
Her father’s experience with political persecution in Taiwan shaped the family’s values of freedom and democracy

Personal Bio
Source: GSTPC Official Pastor Page

籍貫 (Ancestral home): 台灣台南 (Tainan, Taiwan)

Pastor Pingtung Lai (賴炳烔)
Pastor Pingtung Lai (賴炳烔, Lai Ping-tung) was a Taiwanese Presbyterian pastor, Bible Society pioneer, and evangelist. He was a student of Dr. Barclay at Tainan Theological College and Seminary (TTCS), built Beigang Church, founded United Bible Societies work in Taiwan, and established Good Friend Mission. His son, Dr. Albert S. Lai (賴信雄), documented this heritage in the Self-Preface material tied to Toward A Community of Hope (1971 / 2025 reprint).

Full name: 賴炳烔 (Lai Ping-tung / Pastor Pingtung Lai)
Era: ~1914–1990s (active ministry c. 1936–1990s)
Geography: Taiwan (Huwei, Chingliao, Beigang, Taichung, Tainan) → assisted US church establishment
Education: TTCS 1932–1936 (student council president 1935–1936); Nanking Theological Seminary
Core roles: Presbyterian pastor; Bible Society founder; evangelist; Good Friend Mission pioneer

Life & Ministry (three stages)

Pastoral ministry — Huwei, Chingliao, Ailan (Wu-niu-lan), Beigang (built church); Centennial Doubling Campaign evangelistic officer; assisted US church planting
Bible missions — founded United Bible Societies work in Taiwan from Beigang, then Taichung office/warehouse; translation/distribution; advisory network including KMT-era Christian officials (e.g. 張群, 周聯華, 馬壽華)
Post-retirement evangelism — Taiwan International Missions; Good Friend Mission (勵友中心) continued by second generation

people/shawna-yang-ryan.title: Shawna Yang Ryan (楊小娜)
people/shawna-yang-ryan.content:
Shawna Yang Ryan (楊小娜)
Shawna Yang Ryan (楊小娜) is a Taiwanese American novelist whose debut novel Green Island (《綠島》) won the 2017 American Book Awards. Her work explores themes of Taiwanese history, diaspora memory, and the immigrant experience.
Identity Snapshot

English: Shawna Yang Ryan
Chinese: 楊小娜
Born: Sacramento, California
Parents: Father — American, served US Air Force in Taichung; Mother — Taiwanese-born, Wai Sheng second-generation from Taichung
Core roles: Novelist, Creative Writing Professor
Notable work: Green Island (《綠島》), 2017 American Book Awards winner; Water Ghosts (Penguin Press 2009)
Education: UC Berkeley (English Literature); UC Davis (MFA Creative Writing); Fulbright Scholar 2002
Heritage: Second-generation Taiwanese American
Geography: United States (California / Hawaii)

Green Island
Shawna Yang Ryan’s novel Green Island (《綠島》) tells the story of a Taiwanese family during the White Terror period (1950s), when political dissidents were imprisoned on Green Island (綠島) off the southeast coast of Taiwan. The novel explores themes of political persecution, family separation, and the long shadow of authoritarian rule on Taiwanese families.
The book was recognized with the 2017 American Book Awards, a prestigious literary honor that celebrates books of merit written by authors of color. This recognition placed Yang Ryan among a distinguished group of Asian American literary voices.
Writing Process
Yang Ryan spent nearly 14 years writing Green Island, from initial concept to publication in 2016 (Knopf). The seed was planted in 1999 when, at age 22, she walked past the 228 Memorial Park in Taipei and was deeply shocked by the exhibits — discovering a suppressed history she had never been taught. She returned to Taiwan in 2002 as a Fulbright Scholar to conduct research, interviewing 228 massacre survivors and their families. She also continued her Mandarin studies in Taipei over three years.
The novel’s title derives from the song “Green Island Night Song” (綠島小夜曲) and carries dual political meanings: the Green Island prison that held political prisoners, and Taiwan’s martial law era that began on May 20, 1949 and entered the “White Terror” period. The story spans three generations of the Taiwanese Cai family, weaving through the 228 Massacre, the Vietnam War, President Chiang Ching-kuo’s visit, the Sino-US diplomatic break, the Wen-shan case, the Beautiful Sunday incident, Taiwan’s lifting of martial law, and other major events.
The unnamed female protagonist — born on the day of the 228 Massacre — narrates the story in first person, covering the period from 1947 to 2013. Yang Ryan chose first-person narration and an unnamed protagonist to reflect the identity confusion many Taiwanese Americans face.
Yang Ryan’s novel was noted by the New York Times and Los Angeles Times, which published book reviews praising its prose and storytelling. A Chinese translation was published in Taiwan by 印刻出版社 in late 2016.
Teaching Career
After receiving her MFA from UC Davis, Yang Ryan taught at City College of San Francisco for eight years, then moved to Honolulu to teach creative writing at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, where she is now a tenured associate professor and director of the Creative Writing Program. She also taught English at several 補習班 (cram schools) while living in Taiwan.
Community Engagement
Yang Ryan has given book talks and readings at nine organizations in the Greater Los Angeles area in March 2017, including events at the Taiwan Cultural Association, the Tustin Taiwanese Presbyterian Church, and the Chinese American Cultural Center. She has spoken at events organized by the Taiwanese American Writers Association, FAPA Southern California Chapter, TAHS, the American Taiwan Research Institute, and various Taiwanese associations in Orange County and Los Angeles. At a March 2017 talk in Pasadena, she told the audience of 500-600 attendees: “This book is written for you.”
Literary Achievement
Yang Ryan’s work is part of a growing body of Taiwanese American literature that seeks to preserve and communicate the historical experiences of the Taiwanese diaspora. Her novel engages with the same history that the Taiwanese American Historical Society (TAHS) was founded to document — the political struggles, the White Terror, and the quest for identity among Taiwanese Americans.
Her appearance in the 2017 TAHS publication (菁英錄) alongside established community leaders and business figures underscores the breadth of Taiwanese American achievement — from corporate CEOs and politicians to literary artists who give voice to the community’s historical memory.
TAHS Connection
Yang Ryan’s profile in the 2017 TAHS publication was prepared by the Taiwanese American Historical Society editors (台美人歷史協會 整理), reflecting the Society’s interest in documenting the contributions of second-generation Taiwanese Americans across all fields, including the arts and literature.

people/su-chun-huai.content:
Su Chun-huai (蘇春槐)
Su Chun-huai (蘇春槐) is a Taiwanese American community leader and the father of Lisa T. Su (蘇姿丰), CEO of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). His profile in the 2017 TAHS Publication was titled “虎爸談虎女” (Tiger Father Talks About Tiger Daughter) — a play on the “tiger parent” concept, but here the father is proud of his daughter’s extraordinary achievements.
Identity Snapshot

English: Su Chun-huai
Chinese: 蘇春槐
Role: Community leader; father of Lisa T. Su (AMD CEO)
Geography: United States (New York area)
Notable: Founding director of the New York Taiwan Association (紐約台灣會館創會理事)
Profile title: 虎爸談虎女 (Tiger Father Talks About Tiger Daughter)
Profile author: 賴慧娜

Background
Su Chun-huai is a community leader who has been actively involved in Taiwanese American organizations. He is a founding director (創會理事) of the New York Taiwan Association (紐約台灣會館), an organization that serves Taiwanese Americans in the New York metropolitan area.
His profile in the 2017 TAHS Publication was notable for its focus on his pride in his daughter Lisa’s achievements as CEO of AMD. The profile highlighted his role as a father who raised a daughter who would go on to become one of the most powerful women in the technology industry.
”虎爸談虎女”
The title “虎爸談虎女” (Tiger Father Talks About Tiger Daughter) was a play on the popular “tiger parent” concept — but in Su Chun-huai’s case, it was the father who was the “tiger” (虎), not the daughter. He was known for his strict parenting and high expectations, which his daughter credited with helping her achieve at the highest levels.
The profile emphasized Su Chun-huai’s role in helping his daughter learn about other fields while helping others — a philosophy of mutual learning and growth.
Community Involvement
Su Chun-huai has been involved in various Taiwanese American community organizations, including:

Founding director, New York Taiwan Association (紐約台灣會館)
Active participant in Taiwanese American community affairs

people/tahs-member-onboarding.title: TAHS member onboarding
people/tahs-member-onboarding.content:
TAHS Member Onboarding
TAHS Member Onboarding is the lightweight induction pathway for people who are being introduced into the Taiwanese American Historical Society (台美人歷史學會 (TAHS)) and the Echopedia historical-record workflow.
This page exists to give public wiki links a stable destination. It does not publish private rosters, internal spreadsheets, personal contact details, or administrative credentials.
Public-Facing Purpose
TAHS onboarding should help a new member understand:

the mission of preserving Taiwanese American historical memory;
the role of Echopedia as a living community archive;
how identity, names, titles, and contribution records are documented carefully;
privacy expectations for personal information, family records, photos, and testimony;
how to contribute corrections, memories, documents, and source leads.

Basic Onboarding Flow

Introduction — a current TAHS/Echopedia contact introduces the person and their historical or volunteer context.
Identity confirmation — names are recorded with Chinese characters, romanized forms, and role context where available.
Consent boundary — the person should understand what can be public, what should remain private, and what needs explicit permission before publication.
Role or title note — if a formal TAHS role is assigned, record the title and scope in the appropriate society or person page only after confirmation.
Contribution path — direct the person to the community contribution hub for memories, photos, documents, corrections, and source leads.
Review loop — published records remain correctable; community members may submit updates as new evidence appears.

Privacy and Safety Rules

Do not publish private phone numbers, private email addresses, home addresses, private spreadsheets, or internal administration links.
Treat family history, immigration stories, political history, church records, and elder testimony with consent-aware care.
Prefer public source links, official documents, and contributor-approved material.
If a person asks for a correction or removal of sensitive information, route it through the Echopedia correction process.

Identity Snapshot

Era: 2026
Geography: United States (Taiwanese American diaspora)
Core roles: community onboarding, identity verification, contribution workflow
