people/tiffany-huang.title: Tiffany Huang (黃咏婷)
people/tiffany-huang.content:
Tiffany Huang (黃咏婷)
Tiffany Frances Huang (黃咏婷) is a Taiwanese American filmmaker and director. She was selected by National Geographic among 100+ applicants to direct a short film as part of their “10 Days of Genius” campaign.
Identity Snapshot

English: Tiffany Frances Huang
Chinese: 黃咏婷
Education: UC San Diego (Media major); Art Center College of Design (Master’s in directing)
Role: Filmmaker, director
Geography: United States (Los Angeles area)
Notable work: National Geographic “10 Days of Genius” campaign — “Moment” short film

Education

UC San Diego — Media major (undergraduate)
Art Center College of Design — Master’s in directing (graduate)

National Geographic: “Moment”
National Geographic commissioned Tiffany to direct a short film as part of their “10 Days of Genius” campaign. The project required her to create a film based on one of Albert Einstein’s ten famous quotes, with the constraint that the film could not exceed 6 minutes. National Geographic provided $15,000 for production.
Tiffany was given only three weeks to prepare, shoot, and edit the film. She chose the quote: “DEATH IS NOT AN END IF WE HAVE LIVED ON OUR CHILDREN.”
Her father had passed away in June 2016, so she wrote a story about his spirit being forever remembered, combined with some of her previous works, and submitted it to National Geographic.
The project was highly competitive — National Geographic received over 100 applicants, and Tiffany was selected from the pool.
Production Details

Director: Tiffany Frances Huang
Cinematographer: Jeremy Lundborg (also a director, Juilliard graduate in dance)
Lead Actress: Chloe Crade (mother is Japanese, father is Irish; Juilliard dance graduate, full-time performer with TV and Broadway experience)
Supporting Role: Tina Chang (張瑞菊) played the mother (she is Tiffany’s mother)
Film Link: youtu.be/raUyrYRiqt4

Results
National Geographic’s Facebook page received over 1 million views for the project. National Geographic also published additional coverage of the project. Tiffany’s film “Moment” was used as the headline image for the coverage.
The new projects led to a significant increase in National Geographic’s Facebook viewership, and injected new creative energy from younger generations into the content.
Previous Work
Before “Moment,” Tiffany had previously created work for church/missionary groups. She used her filming in Africa (where she had worked with a church evangelism group) to apply to Art Center College of Design for her master’s program.

people/wang-gui-rong.title: Wang Gui-rong (王桂榮)
people/wang-gui-rong.content:
Wang Gui-rong (王桂榮)
Wang Gui-rong (1931–2012), also known in English as Kenjohn Wang, was a Taiwanese American entrepreneur, philanthropist, and community leader. He built a hotel and real estate empire in Southern California, founded the Taiwanese American Foundation (TAF), and served in multiple advisory roles to the governments of Taiwan and the United States. He is widely regarded as one of the most generous benefactors in the Taiwanese American community.
Identity Snapshot

English: Wang Gui-rong / Kenjohn Wang
Chinese: 王桂榮
Born: 1931, Taiwan (under Japanese rule)
Died: 2012-02-11, Taipei Medical University Hospital, age 81–82
Citizenship: United States (naturalized 1979-08-24)
Spouse: 王賽美 (Jacqueline Wang)
Children: Three sons — Kenneth, John, Michael
Roles: Entrepreneur; hotel developer; philanthropist; community leader; public affairs advocate
Organizations: Taiwanese American Foundation (TAF); LA Taiwan Center; FAPA; FAPA; Taiwanese Chambers of Commerce

Early Life
Wang Gui-rong was born in 1931 in Taiwan, then under Japanese colonial rule. He attended the Junior College of Administration of Taiwan (now part of National Taipei University) and graduated in 1951. He then joined the military, serving as a lieutenant translator for the U.S. Military Assistance Advisory Group (MAAG) at the Tainan air base from 1955–1956 — a role that established his first connections with Americans.
His future wife, 王賽美 (Jacqueline Wang), was studying at 靜宜英專 (now 靜宜 University, then a junior college in Taichung) and worked at the Taipei American School library and as an elementary school teacher. They married and built their early lives around Taiwan’s English-language and military-adjacent institutions.
Wang originally continued his family’s international trade, Western medicine manufacturing, and import-export businesses in Taiwan. In 1965, he began graduate studies in politics at Kansas State University, then transferred to the University of Texas at Austin for a PhD. Realizing the practical demands of supporting a family, he switched to accounting and eventually opened a CPA firm in Washington, D.C.
Immigration to the United States
Wang’s decision to immigrate was driven by geopolitical fear. In July 1971, Henry Kissinger secretly visited Beijing on behalf of President Nixon. In October 1971, the UN expelled the Chiang Kai-shek government’s representative. Wang recalled: “Friends told each other [that the Chiang regime was expelled from the UN] and all believed Taiwan would fall into chaos.” His fear that Taiwan might fall under Chinese Communist rule was shared by most Taiwanese residents at the time.
Wang and his wife initially planned to immigrate to Paraguay. In 1972, one year after the Shanghai Communique, they migrated to Paraguay. However, while transiting through the United States on their way to South America, they stopped in California for half a year. Despite having no legal status at the time, they enrolled their three children in a nearby elementary school. The principal, moved by compassion, allowed the children to attend and even provided school bus transportation, free lunches, and a dedicated English teacher. Wang later described this experience as “imagine something so wonderful happening in a foreign land — I suddenly wondered if America was the paradise described in Buddhist scriptures.”
This experience established Wang’s deep affection for America and resolved his commitment to give back. He later wrote: “I resolved to earn money, pay taxes, earn more, and pay more taxes, to repay this warm society.”
They ultimately abandoned their Paraguay plan and applied for immigration to the United States — a decision Wang regarded as one of the most significant and correct choices of his life.
Hotel Empire
After settling in California, Wang began his business career in the hospitality industry. In 1974, he purchased his first hotel, the Newland Apartment Motel in Westminster, Orange County. The family worked together — Wang described it as “sweat and toil” (胼手胝足) — and the first year’s profits far exceeded expectations.
In 1975, Wang purchased the long-neglected Outrigger Inn in Long Beach, California. He invested heavily in renovations and operations, transforming the property completely. This hotel became the cornerstone of his empire: he joined the Ramada Inn chain, and Wang later refused lucrative buyout offers because of his special attachment to the property. He expanded it into a mid-to-large hotel, with the ground floor as commercial space and the upper floors housing the Wang family enterprise headquarters.
His hotel empire grew to include:

Ramada Inn / Outrigger Inn (Long Beach) — the flagship
Holiday Inn (Montebello, purchased 1978-07)
Atrium Hotel
Additional properties in Southern California

Wang earned the nickname “旅館大王” (Hotel King) among Taiwanese American business circles. During the 1973–1978 period, when Taiwan’s international situation deteriorated and the U.S. economy was in recession, many Taiwanese business leaders and military officials’ children came to Southern California seeking guidance. Wang welcomed all of them, shared his business secrets freely, and became known as a generous mentor.
Philanthropy and Community Leadership
Wang’s philanthropy was extraordinary in scale and scope. He focused on two areas: giving back to his new country (America) and to his homeland (Taiwan).
Taiwanese American Foundation (TAF)
In 1982, Wang donated $1 million to establish the Taiwanese American Foundation (TAF), which earned him the title “The Nobel of Taiwan” (台灣的諾貝爾). TAF was created to honor outstanding individuals who “care about Taiwan and identify Taiwan as their homeland.” From 1983 onward, laureates included 廖述宗, 柏楊, 李登輝, 彭明敏, 李遠哲, 蘭大弼, and many others from around the world.
LA Taiwan Center
In 1988, Wang donated his property to establish the Los Angeles Taiwan Center (大洛杉磯台灣會館) in Rosemead, California. His vision was: “I always had a wish that Los Angeles would have a Taiwan Center as a home for Taiwanese organizations, a spiritual fortress to promote our culture, bring it into mainstream American society, give back to American society, and raise the status of Taiwanese people in America.”
USC Scholarship
In 1997, he established the Kenjohn Wang Scholarship at the University of Southern California (USC).
Other Contributions

Founded the Taiwan Hotel and Motel Association of Southern California (1974)
Founded the Taiwanese Chambers of Commerce of North America (1987)
Funded and published a commerce-oriented Taiwanese American community newspaper (1980)
Appointed to the Finance Committee by DNC Chairman Ronald H. Brown (1989)
President of FAPA (Formosan Association for Public Affairs) (1989)
Decade Award from the White House (via Asia-Pacific American Heritage Committee)
Member of the President’s Advisory Board under President Chen Shui-bian (2004–2005)

Political Advocacy
Wang was deeply involved in Taiwanese American political organizing. He served as:

President of FAPA (Formosan Association for Public Affairs), a lobby arm for Taiwanese Americans
Member of the Finance Committee, Democratic National Committee (1989)
Appointed to the President’s Advisory Board by President Chen Shui-bian (2004–2005)
Helped organize Taiwanese American political participation in U.S. electoral processes

He understood “the rules of the game” in American society and believed that political engagement was essential to elevating the status of Taiwanese Americans in mainstream society.
Death and Legacy
Wang Gui-rong died on 2012-02-11 at Taipei Medical University Hospital in Taipei, where he was receiving medical treatment. At the time of his death, he was still a U.S. citizen. He was 81–82 years old.
He left behind two books, including his memoirs published in 1999. His three sons — Kenneth, John, and Michael — now manage the Kenjohn Group, which includes his hotel businesses, real estate investments, and trade operations in both America and Taiwan.
Source Notes and Confidence

people/wang-neng-xiang.title: Wang Neng-xiang (王能祥)
people/wang-neng-xiang.content:
Wang Neng-xiang (王能祥)
Wang Neng-xiang (王能祥, 1933–) is a Taiwanese American CPA, Taiwan democracy lobbyist, and community leader based in Washington, D.C. He has been a pioneer in advocating for Taiwan’s international visibility and democratic movement in the United States for over 40 years.
Identity Snapshot

English: Wang Neng-xiang / Neng-Hsiang Wang
Chinese: 王能祥
Born: 1933, Nanzikeng (楠仔坑), Kaohsiung Prefecture, Taiwan
Era: 1933–present (now in his eighties)
Profession: CPA; CPA firm owner
Role: Taiwan democracy lobbyist; community leader
Geography: Washington, D.C. (since 1972)
Organizations: WUFI Foreign Affairs Dept (1973–1977); Overseas Alliance for Democratic Movement in Taiwan (1977–1985)
Elder: Taiwanese Presbyterian Church near Washington, D.C.
Profile authors: 楊嘉猷 (創會會長) and 周威霖

Early Life
Wang Neng-xiang was born in 1933 in Nanzikeng, Kaohsiung Prefecture, Taiwan, into a Christian family. At age 9, he was denied schooling by the Japanese colonial master and spent three years roaming alone on the mountains. Despite this early hardship, he later entered the Kaohsiung Commercial School, and after some twists and turns, graduated from the Politics Department of Taiwan University in 1959.
Education and Career
In 1965, Wang left Taiwan to study in the United States, following the pattern of Taiwanese youth elites of that era. He first attended Kansas State University (Manhattan) for a master’s degree in political science. In 1967, he transferred to the University of Texas at Austin for a PhD in political science. Two years later, out of practical considerations, he switched to accounting.
He eventually opened a CPA firm in Washington, D.C., where he has practiced to the present day.
Taiwan Democracy Advocacy
Wang Neng-xiang is a lifelong fighter for Taiwan’s international visibility and an end to Taiwan’s colonial status. He has been based in Washington, D.C. since 1972 — the time when Washington became the center of international power play after World War II.
WUFI Foreign Affairs Department (1973–1977)
Wang served as Head of Foreign Affairs’ Department for World United Formosans for Independence (WUFI) from 1973 to 1977.
Overseas Alliance for Democratic Movement in Taiwan (1977–1985)
He served as Secretary General of the Overseas Alliance for Democratic Movement in Taiwan from 1977 to 1985.
Key Hearings
Wang was involved in holding four landmark hearings:

1965 — Hearing at Kansas State University to seek denial for Chinese Student Association’s representation of Taiwan and to seek acceptance for Formosan Student Association as its lawful representation
1977 — Hearing at the U.S. House of Representatives to investigate KMT’s human rights violations
1980 — Hearing at the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives to offer a legal framework for Taiwan, which led to the birth of the Taiwan Relations Act and the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT)
1994 — Hearing at the House of Representatives to offer a license to anti-KMT television station, which led to the birth of FTV (Formosa Television) in Taiwan

Taiwan Lobby
Wang was involved in discussions about restructuring the “China Lobby.” When the KMT当局 (KMT authorities) wanted to rebrand the China Lobby under the name “Taiwan Lobby,” Wang presented them with a difficult challenge — essentially a “soft nail” (軟釘子) that made the KMT abandon the plan.
Community Leadership
Wang is a devout Christian and has been an elder of the Taiwanese Presbyterian Church near Washington, D.C., which he helped build with many Taiwanese American church members through fundraising and contributions. He has served as an elder of the church for many years, and Taiwanese Americans or Taiwanese immigrants in the greater Washington area who see him refer to him as “長老” (Elder).
Legacy
Wang Neng-xiang is now in his eighties and still in excellent health. In addition to busily running his CPA firm, he continues to pursue Taiwan’s international visibility and aspire to end Taiwan’s colonial sufferings. His profile was co-authored by 楊嘉猷 (創會會長 of TAHS) and 周威霖, describing him as “心繫台灣、老驥扶櫪” (heart set on Taiwan, veteran horse still galloping).

people/yang-jia-you.title: Charles Yang (楊嘉猷)
people/yang-jia-you.content:
Charles Yang (楊嘉猷)
Charles Yang (楊嘉猷) is the founding president (創會會長) of the Taiwanese American Historical Society (TAHS / 台美人歷史協會). He is a community leader, essayist, and advocate for Taiwanese American identity and history.
Identity Snapshot

English: Charles Yang
Chinese: 楊嘉猷
Role: Founding President, TAHS (台美人歷史協會創會會長)
Geography: Southern California (Los Angeles area)
Key work: 緣起與展望 (Origins and Prospects) — founding essay of TAHS
Era: Active 2013–present (TAHS founding); 2017 publication year
Organizations: Taiwanese American Historical Society (TAHS)

TAHS Founding
Charles Yang was the driving force behind the founding of the Taiwanese American Historical Society. In 2013, he organized a preparatory meeting on August 28 in Southern California, which was attended by 黃根深, 周實, 鄭炳全, 鄭英松, 王廷宜, 楊子清, 洪珠美, 陳隆, 周威霖, and others.
The founding conference was held on December 11, 2013, at the Hilton San Gabriel, where the organization was formally registered as a nonprofit public society in the United States, based in Southern California with the aim of expanding nationwide.
Founding Essay: 緣起與展望
Yang wrote the founding essay “緣起與展望” (Origins and Prospects), which outlined the five core principles (五大信念) of the “台灣精神史觀” (Taiwanese Spirit Historical Perspective) that TAHS was founded to promote:

歷史傳承 (Historical Heritage) — Taiwanese diaspora should document biographies and org histories for identity and solidarity
族群榮譽 (Ethnic Honor) — Building individual dignity is the true value of life and the basic creed of overall honor
全民團結 (National Unity) — Unity is based on people’s “harmony” — “家和為興、友和為貴、國和為天”
社會責任 (Social Responsibility) — Taiwanese Americans have dual hearts and dual responsibilities: to America and to Taiwan
前途希望 (Future Hope) — Hope is the combination of “expectation” and “confidence”

His essay argues that the Taiwanese diaspora should document biographies and org histories for identity and solidarity, and that second-generation Taiwanese Americans should network so youth feel less isolated and take pride in Taiwanese identity.
Five Principles of TAHS
Yang’s founding essay sets out five “台灣精神史觀” (Taiwanese Spirit Historical Perspective) principles:

歷史傳承 (Historical Heritage): Immigrant nations, new continent — America is the melting pot of all ethnicities. Taiwanese Americans should pass on their good culture and capable history generation after generation.
族群榮譽 (Ethnic Honor): Building individual dignity is the true value of life and the basic creed of overall honor.
全民團結 (National Unity): Unity is based on people’s “harmony.” As 蔣渭水 said: “同胞要團結，團結真有力” (Fellow countrymen, unite — unity is truly powerful).
社會責任 (Social Responsibility): Taiwanese Americans have two hearts — one for America, one for Taiwan. They have a dual responsibility.
前途希望 (Future Hope): Hope is the combination of “expectation” and “confidence.”

Health Issues and Franklin Ping Cheng
Due to physical health conditions, including two major surgeries, Charles Yang stepped aside from his role as TAHS president. Franklin Ping Cheng, who had served one year as vice-president, assumed the presidency in 2014. Yang recovered within a year and continued to help the Society, but Franklin served as president during the critical period when the 2017 yearbook was produced.
Legacy
Yang’s legacy is the establishment of TAHS as an organization dedicated to documenting Taiwanese American history and celebrating the community’s achievements. His founding essay remains the philosophical foundation of the organization.
Source Notes and Confidence

people/yang-xin.title: Yang Hsin (楊信)
people/yang-xin.content:
Yang Hsin (楊信)
Yang Hsin (楊信, born 1944), also known in English as Jackson Yang, is a Taiwanese American entrepreneur and community leader. He is the CEO of Seville Classics, Inc., a globally leading innovator and manufacturer in housewares and storage, generating annual revenue of over $200 million. Seville was awarded “Vendor of the Year” by Walmart. He is also the Chairman of FGB (First Guangfu Bank), a community bank focused on serving small businesses and individuals in Southern California.
Identity Snapshot

English: Yang Hsin / Jackson Yang
Chinese: 楊信
Born: 1944, Puxin Township (埔心鄉), Changhua County, Taiwan (year of the end of WWII)
Family: Youngest of 7 siblings
Spouse: 何巧玲 (He Qiaoling)
Education: Elementary school only (dropped out after 1 semester of middle school)
Core roles: CEO, Seville Classics, Inc.; Chairman, FGB community bank
Geography: Southern California (Los Angeles area)
Organizations: Seville Classics; FGB Bank; Taiwanese Chambers of Commerce; World Taiwanese Chambers of Commerce

Early Life
Yang Hsin was born in 1944 in Puxin Township, Changhua County — the year before the end of World War II. His family had 7 siblings; he was the youngest and most pampered. His mother never attended school but was a hardworking rural woman who managed the household with great frugality.
When Yang was in 6th grade, his father died suddenly. The family lost its center of gravity. His mother managed alone, borrowing money from neighbors to pay his school registration fees. She rented out the family’s small plot of farmland and sold the rice harvest to pay debts. Yang’s meals were mostly sweet potatoes with a little white rice — he was too embarrassed to open his lunchbox at school because most of it was sweet potato.
His first real memory of white rice was at a classmate’s temple festival, where he was invited to stay overnight and given a white-rice lunchbox. He still remembers that feeling vividly.
He passed the exam for middle school but attended only one semester before dropping out. He could not bear to see his mother borrowing from neighbors every semester for his fees, and decided to become self-reliant.
First Job: Soy Sauce Factory
His first job was at an uncle’s soy sauce factory in Yunlin, where his main task was washing recycled old soy sauce bottles. The bottles were returned by villagers and were very dirty — they had to be soaked overnight in water, then scrubbed to remove soy sauce residue.
That winter was particularly cold. Yang kept his hands in cold water all day, and they became severely frostbitten — swollen, blistered, and rotting. When he returned home for Chinese New Year, his mother saw his hands and could not bear it. She decided to send him to Taipei to learn trade instead.
Taipei Trade Company
In 1961, at age 17, Yang took a slow train from Yuanlin Station to Taipei — a 5-hour journey standing room only, since it was just after Chinese New Year and the trains were packed.
In Taipei, he worked at a small international trade company on Yanping North Road. The company had only two people: the owner and Yang. His job was to draft English product introduction letters. He also opened and checked the company’s mailbox at the Post Office every morning and evening — international trade at that time used postal boxes as the primary communication address.
The owner’s wife helped another company with bookkeeping. Yang learned the importance of English and, despite his meager salary of 80 NTD per month (less than the 200-300 NTD evening class fee), enrolled at “Melton” (美爾頓), an English cram school.
After nearly 4 years, Yang advanced from a junior clerk to a “small adult” (junior staff). The company specialized in canned food exports — pineapple, orange, lychee, mushroom, bamboo shoot, and asparagus — mainly to Germany and the United States. Taiwanese countryside mushrooms had low production costs, and the profit margin was excellent: about $10+ per box. The company made a lot of money.
Military Service and Independent Business
After military service, Yang’s friend Huang Shicheng (黃石城, later County Magistrate of Changhua) encouraged him to start his own trade company. Yang had no capital, so he organized a “rotating savings association” (招會仔) — 20 people contributing 500 NTD each, totaling 10,000 NTD. With this money, he bought an Underwood typewriter, rented a small office on Chongqing South Road, and began his international trade career.
Immigration to the United States
In 1984, Yang and his wife He Qiaoling visited the United States for summer vacation. Their children loved America so much they said they didn’t want to return to Taiwan. The children’s longing for America, combined with his wife’s “keen insight” about the US, led to a firm decision to immigrate.
Yang’s wife, 何巧玲, first brought the 4 children to the US. Yang remained in Taiwan for two years as an “air traveler” (空中飛人), gradually shifting his business center to America.
In 1986, Yang joined his family in the US and settled down, starting a new chapter of his career.
Building Seville Classics
The Swap Meet Years
When Yang first arrived in America, everything was unfamiliar. Fortunately, his good friend Mr. Lin Jilong (林基龍) and his wife helped them find housing and settle in.
Yang discovered that his company in America, run by a manager, had unsold products堆积 (piling up) in the warehouse. He had to sell them himself — loading products onto his truck and taking them to swap meets (跳蚤市場) every weekend.
He quickly discovered that not all products sold well — there was a gap between supply and demand. “What should I sell?” was the key question. Yang spent two years at swap meets, learning American consumer preferences. He also frequently traveled to Taiwan and China to select products to test the US market.
The Seat Cushion Breakthrough
At a Guangzhou trade fair in China, Yang saw a wooden bead seat cushion — the kind taxi drivers in Taiwan used. He thought: “America has so many cars, but no similar product. This is worth trying.” He bought 2,000 seat cushions for over $10,000.
When he brought them to his American sales representative, he was met with cold rejection: “Americans won’t buy this.”
Yang was discouraged but had no choice — the goods were already shipped. He decided to sell them at the swap meet himself to test the market.
He bought two used car seats from an old car lot, placed the wooden bead cushions on them, and put round bead cushions on top, selling them with the selling points of “cooling” and “massage.” Customers could sit and feel the product firsthand.
The result: the cushions sold incredibly well — dozens per day. Each cushion cost $5 to make, and he sold them for $15.
Comfortbeads and Global Scale
Yang named the product “Comfortbeads” (舒適珠) and packaged them in beautifully designed hard boxes with pictures showing the product installed on car seats. He priced them at $12.99.
He approached BJ’s Wholesale Club, a home goods chain with over a dozen stores on the East Coast. He negotiated a “two-week trial” — if the product didn’t sell, he would take it back unconditionally.
Two weeks after shipping, Yang received a call: the client wanted immediate restocking because Comfortbeeds sold so well, even surprising the store. Yang immediately bought a ticket to China, found the manufacturer, and ordered over 7,000 units. The first shipping container was imported in bulk. Packaging boxes were printed in Taiwan and assembled/shipped from Los Angeles.
After the product became popular, Price Club (the predecessor of Costco) and Walmart also began selling it, opening the entire US big-box store market.
Quality Crisis and Recovery
Not all experiences were smooth. Each seat cushion had over 500 wooden beads strung together with nylon thread by hand. The Chinese-made nylon thread was not strong enough — American customers were larger, and when they sat on the cushions, the thread broke and beads scattered, leading to high return rates that damaged his reputation.
Yang rushed back to Taiwan, found high-quality, strong beef tendon thread, and had it used on the production line. This improved product quality, reduced defect rates, and consolidated his reputation.
At peak, he imported over 200,000 units per week from China. The large volume drove costs down — each unit cost as little as $1.50. He sold to stores for $7-8, and they retailed at $9.99. In 1988-1990, $9.99 was an incredibly cheap product for American consumers, so it sold fast.
Comfortbeads sold 10 million units across the US in 3 years, earning Yang his “first pot of gold” in America and laying the foundation for his business.
Seville Classics, Inc.
Over the years, Yang built Seville Classics, Inc. into a globally leading innovator and manufacturer in housewares and storage. The company generates annual revenue of over $200 million and was awarded “Vendor of the Year” by Walmart.
Banking and Community Leadership
FGB Community Bank
Yang is the Chairman of FGB (First Guangfu Bank), a community bank mainly focusing on serving small businesses and individuals in Southern California. In 2012, FGB ranked first among the nation’s best forming community banks by SNL Financial. As of December 31, 2016, FGB’s total assets exceeded $840 million, operating 4 branches across the Greater San Gabriel Valley and Orange County.
Chamber of Commerce Leadership

Los Angeles Chinese American Chamber of Commerce: President (2004)
Taiwanese Chambers of Commerce of North America: President (initiated “Second Generation Assistance” program to introduce young Taiwanese Americans to the real world)
World Taiwanese Chambers of Commerce (WTCC): President (2013–2014)
World United Council of Chinese Chambers of Commerce: 20th President (2006)

WTCC Presidency
Yang’s WTCC presidency was marked by grand events:

2006 (19th WTCC): Hosted in Hawaii with help from the Hawaiian Chinese Chamber of Commerce. Despite the high cost, Yang covered all expenses. The event coincided with Halloween, and Yang chartered a boat for a sea celebration. Attendees found it unforgettable.
2007: Second session in Dallas; annual meeting scheduled for 2008 in Los Angeles.
2008 (20th WTCC): Hosted in Los Angeles. Yang organized a three-day, two-night Mexico cruise specifically offering discounted rates for second-generation youth members. Many young members joined, and several couples met on the cruise. Yang served as their wedding witness — a story still told in the community. He was frequently asked to organize similar cruises.
2013 (19th WTCC): Hosted at the Grand Hyatt in Taipei. Yang invested $70,000-80,000 to upgrade the stage per the requirements of popular Taiwanese rock band “Power Station” (動力火車), producing a spectacular evening where attendees waved electronic glow sticks. The event was described as “high to the sky.”

TPP Lobbying Trip
One of Yang’s most significant initiatives as WTCC President was the “Washington DC TPP Knock-on-Door Tour” (華府 TPP 叩門之旅).
Understanding the importance of the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement for Taiwan and US shared interests, Yang broke precedent by leading a delegation to Washington DC to meet with US Congress members and officials — instead of the traditional Beijing visits that previous WTCC Presidents had conducted.
The proposal received enthusiastic support from the Overseas Community Affairs Council (僑務委員會), Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Los Angeles, and Washington office.
Thanks to Taiwanese Americans’ strong support for local Congress members, Yang’s delegation had deep relationships. Lawyer Hu Weigang (胡維剛) and his wife provided significant assistance.
Upon arrival at Capitol Hill, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Ed Royce hosted a welcome reception in the House chamber for the delegation, with nearly 30 Congress members attending — a grand and impressive event.
Personal Philosophy
Yang credits his life journey to three sources of help:

His mother’s love — sent him to Taipei to learn trade
His wife’s vision — decided to move to America to open new horizons
A friend’s help — “when far from home, a friend makes all the difference”

He describes his life as having always been blessed by “noble people” (貴人) who helped him at critical moments.
Source Notes and Confidence

Spiritual call amid cultural transition
From ethnic church to missional community — FPCLA as a “mission base”
Hopeful community theology
Unfinished mission across generations

sources/toward-a-community-of-hope.content:
Toward A Community of Hope
Full title: Toward A Community Of Hope — A Mission to Formosan Community in Los Angeles
Author: Dr. Albert S. Lai (賴信雄)
Type: Doctor of Ministry dissertation (San Francisco Theological Seminary), December 1971
Republication: 2025 (50th anniversary), Taiwan Church Press + NTPC + Tainan East Gate Barclay History Education Promotion
Identity Snapshot

Era: Written 1971; rediscovered/translated 2022–2025; reprinted 2025
Geography: Los Angeles Formosan community; Taiwanese American Presbyterian history
Core roles: Primary source on FPCLA founding; theology of “community of hope”

Why it matters
This is the foundational written account of the first Taiwanese Presbyterian church in North America (FPCLA) and a theological vision of the church as a hopeful / missional community, not only an ethnic haven.
